title: Ambulance ramping data casts doubt over LNP promise to reduce wait times
text:
Queues of long-wait ambulance patients outside many of Queensland's major hospital emergency departments have barely budged in the last two years.

The latest Queensland Health performance data for August shows statewide ambulance ramping is sitting at 42 per cent across Queensland's 26 top public hospital emergency departments (ED).

That means 42 per cent of patients who arrive at those hospitals by ambulance are waiting longer than 30 minutes to be transferred off a stretcher into an ED.

In July, ambulance ramping across the same hospitals stood at 38.7 per cent — 3.3 percentage points better than the August figures.

Ambulance ramping figures have barely budged in the last two years. (ABC News: Scott Kyle)

The numbers are only marginally better than the August before the Crisafulli Government came to power in 2024, when ramping stood at 43.9 per cent.

In 2025 — Queensland's worst flu season on record — August ramping rates were at 45.6 per cent under the LNP Government.

Pressure to reduce ramping

The latest August data comes just ahead of the halfway mark in the Crisafulli Government's first four-year term and on the back of a late flu season.

It puts in serious doubt the Premier's commitment ahead of the 2024 election to get ambulance ramping down to under 30 per cent before the 2028 poll.

Health Minister Tim Nicholls is under pressure to get ramping under 30 per cent before 2028. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

The latest figures pile more pressure on Health Minister Tim Nicholls after Premier David Crisafulli tied his cabinet future to cutting ambulance ramping to below 30 per cent before the next election.

Opposition leader Steven Miles predicted ramping figures would continue to worsen.

"You can't fix ramping while not delivering growth funding to our hospitals, not having a workforce plan, and not building the new beds that are needed," he said.

"The government still hasn't delivered a workforce plan to deliver the staffing those hospitals need and of course, they've delayed the build of new beds that would provide some relief to the bed block that is choking our emergency departments."

Opposition leader Steven Miles said ramping figures were likely to worsen. (ABC News: Lucas Hill)

August ramping figures show hospitals in the Metro South Health region are particularly struggling.

Logan Hospital, south of Brisbane, recorded ramping levels at 61.8 per cent and at the Princess Alexandra Hospital, more than half of the patients arriving at the emergency department by ambulance were ramped for more than half an hour.

In the regions, Cairns Hospital ramping was 45.6 per cent in August, Bundaberg Hospital was only marginally better at 44.7 per cent, and at Rockhampton Hospital, it was 39.1 per cent.

Gold Coast University Hospital just snuck in under the 30 per cent target, recording 28.9 per cent — a huge improvement on when the Miles Government was in power when ramping was at 48.2 per cent in August 2024 — two months before the Queensland election.

Ambulance ramping at Ipswich Hospital has been cut to 34.5 per cent since August 2024. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Ambulance ramping at Ipswich Hospital, west of Brisbane, has also turned around in the past two years.

In August 2024, a whopping 63.5 per cent of patients arriving by ambulance to the hospital, were ramped for more than the recommended benchmark of 30 minutes.

That has been cut to 34.5 per cent on the back of the Mater Springfield Hospital opening in May.

A spokeswoman for acting Health and Ambulance Services Minister Dale Last said the 2026 August ramping data was the lowest August figures in five years.

In August 2021, ambulance ramping was 38.7 per cent at Queensland’s major public hospitals.

This year’s data comes amid a record high 211,664 presentations to Queensland public hospital emergency departments in August.

title: How the card surcharge ban could change our relationship with cash
text:
With the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) ban on card surcharges now in effect you might start seeing local businesses offering discounts if you pay in cash.

Cash payments in Australia are much less common than they were a decade ago, but the RBA's latest data showed a slight uptick in cash use in 2025.

How could the ban on card surcharges impact how cash is used in Australia?

How often do people use cash?

This graph from the RBA's 2025 Consumer Payments Survey tracks the percentage of Australians who use cash in a typical week.

As you can see, 2025's figure of 50 per cent is much lower than the 97 per cent in 2007.

But it's slightly higher than 2022's figure of 47 per cent.

Will we move back to cash?

John Hawkins, a senior economic lecturer at the University of Canberra, doesn't expect cash use to skyrocket.

"From January the government has required most grocery stores and petrol stations to accept cash, which may see some modest increase in its use," Dr Hawkins says.

"On the other hand, about 20 per cent of consumers say they used cash to avoid card surcharges.

"As these no longer apply we could see some drop in cash use."

Loading...

Angel Zhong, a finance professor at RMIT, says she would be surprised if the surcharge ban reverses the long-term trend of card payments.

"I expect a modest uptick [in cash use] mostly at the margins: the café, the barber or the tradie offering a few per cent off for cash," Professor Zhong says.

"Australians moved to cards and mobile wallets mainly because of convenience, speed and record keeping, not because of price.

"A small discount at a handful of businesses is unlikely to change entrenched habits for most people."

Government backs down on ATO credit card ban The federal government will temporarily cover credit card surcharges after businesses warned that losing the payment option would put them under pressure.

Data from the RBA's 2025 survey showed people aged 65 and older were the most likely to use cash.

Cash might also still be preferred by people in regional areas with limited bank access or poor internet signal, people managing tight budgets, and people who have privacy concerns.

Professor Zhong says the goal should be to continue offering people the choice of using cash or paying by card.

Why would cafés offer cash discounts?

Professor Zhong sees cash discounts as a sign of how much pressure small businesses are under.

"The RBA paired the ban with a cut to interchange fees, which was meant to soften the blow by lowering what businesses pay to accept cards," she says.

"But interchange is only one part of the cost.

"Small businesses typically pay their payment service provider a bundled rate, and there's no guarantee that the interchange savings flow through to that rate."

Card payments are much more common than they were in 2007. (AAP: Dan Peled)

While big businesses could leverage their bargaining power to negotiate savings in their contracts, smaller businesses don't have that option.

And that means losing the ability to surcharge while missing out on a drop in costs.

"Against thin margins and rising operating costs, offering a discount for cash is one of the few ways a small business can steer customers toward a cheaper payment method," Professor Zhong says.

Are cash discounts legal?

Yes.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) says businesses can offer discounts to customers paying via particular means such as cash or PayID, but there are a few rules.

In charts: Cash use in Australia has increased Cash use has dropped by more than 50 per cent in almost 20 years. But there has been a slight increase in cash payments since 2022.

Discounts should be clearly disclosed before payment and they have to advertise the non-discounted price.

They're not allowed to display the discounted price more prominently than the full price.

Is it legal to hike prices to cover the surcharge ban?

Yes, but there are rules about how businesses label these price hikes.

"They must not mislead consumers about prices, including about the reasons for any price increases," the ACCC says.

An example of this might be a nursery that used to apply a 1 per cent credit card surcharge for its products.

Price hikes are legal, but businesses have to be careful with their labelling. (ABC News: Dannielle Maguire)

To compensate for that cost, they might increase the cost of a $10 pot plant to $10.10.

But let's say the nursery owner decides that, while they're setting new figures, they'll increase the pot plant's price to $12 to cover the rise in their electricity and water bills.

That's totally legal too.

But they aren't allowed to say the price increase from $10 to $12 is because of the ban.

"This will be misleading because the price increase also reflects other business costs, not just the cost of accepting card payments," the ACCC says.

title: The fruit and vegetables to look out for this month
text:
Asparagus is "absolutely sublime" at the moment, according to green grocer Jo Toscano.

Snow peas are also in season during spring. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Asparagus, snow peas and garden peas are increasingly prominent on shelves as spring sets in.

While no-one doubts the convenience of frozen peas, Effie Ramos from organic market garden Remi's Patch in Naarm/Melbourne says there's something special about the ritual of slowing down and popping the pods open yourself.

University of Newcastle nutrition professor Clare Collins says shopping seasonally can help us to introduce variety into our diets.

"If you eyeball all the veggies and fruit, look at what hasn't visited your trolley for a few weeks," she says.

What can you look for?

Vegetables:

Asparagus

Garden peas

Snow peas

Broad beans, including broad bean tips

Broccoli

Cauliflower

Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli and bok choy

Capsicum

Beetroot

Fresh garlic

Celery

Fruit:

Citrus, such as alfourer mandarins, navel and blood oranges

Mangoes, as availability increases

Asparagus, peas and broad beans

Asparagus is expected to peak in mid-to-late October, Ms Toscano says.

People tend to avoid the thick asparagus spears, but she says they're "juicy and full of flavour".

Four spring asparagus recipes From one-pot pasta to a crunchy green salad, these easy recipes will put spring asparagus on your weeknight menu.

White asparagus doesn't offer the "great value" of green asparagus, Ms Toscano says "it is divine". She recommends peeling it as the exterior can be "quite fibrous".

Dr Collins says asparagus works well in an omelette, quiche or with a simple cheese sauce.

Garden peas are also in season.

"Fresh peas sort of stay elevated in price but when they're good they're really good and it's worth it," Ms Toscano says.

When garden peas are fresh and young, she suggests using the pods (after they've been shelled) to flavour homemade vegetable stock or blitzing and sieving that mixture to make an intense pea-flavoured cooking liquid.

Broad beans are also "awesome" right now, Ms Toscano says.

Ms Ramos says the leafy green tip of the broad beans have been popular and are "really good, fresh in a salad".

Effie Ramos says there is nothing as good as peas when they are at their peak. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm )

Brassicas and Asian greens (again)

Broccoli and cauliflower "are pretty good value" and Asian greens such as Chinese broccoli are another good buy, Ms Toscano says.

Dr Collins says brassicas, including cauliflower, broccoli and cabbage, can be divisive because they can taste bitter to "super tasters" — people with a more sensitive sense of taste.

"But the good news, especially for parents, is that [through] repeated exposure you increase your tolerance," she says.

Avoid overcooking the produce and try roasting it or masking the flavour with something like a cheese sauce if someone you are cooking for finds it bitter, she suggests.

Jo Toscano says carrots are available year-round, but they are "unbelievable at the moment as well". (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Seeing red (capsicum and beetroot)

Ms Toscano says lots of red capsicums are coming from Queensland and that there are "bargains to be had" over the next couple of weeks.

Dr Collins says you can use affordable capsicums and Asian greens in stir-fries.

Ms Ramos says it's a good time for beetroot, which can be added to salads, raw or cooked.

"A lot of people sort of underestimate the power of the leaves of the beets. You can have them raw, or I just blanch them with a little bit of olive oil," she says.

Ms Ramos expects an abundance of spring onions, coriander, parsley, which will decrease prices.

October fruit offerings

Grapes have started but they're still very expensive, Ms Toscano says, and the first stone fruit will begin appearing this month.

"With the confluence of WA and Queensland mango seasons in a few weeks, prices are expected to fall," she says.

Cathy Senn from Sensational Berries in Naarm/Melbourne says supplies of Victorian berries will increase as the month continues, adding to those coming from northern Australia.

Lemon delicious pudding A hot pudding doused in cream is always welcome in cooler months.

"Starting with the strawberries and then we'll go on to raspberries and then later on we'll have the blueberries come on and then the strawberries, the blackberries after that," she says.

Citrus varieties are "diminishing", Ms Senn says, pointing to her "about finished" blood oranges, cara cara oranges and ruby grapefruits.

Dr Collins says at this time of year you can often buy bags of great value lemons and oranges. If she's got people coming over, she likes to cook her lemon-and-orange delicious.

"You use the rind, the more rind the better," she says.

Separating the egg white from the egg yolks is "the tricky bit", but it's also a good opportunity to teach kids or grandkids how to do it.

title: Firmus wobbles have opponents relieved, critics questioning deals
text:
The news of data centre operator Firmus's share market float being pulled has been met with disappointment from some investors.

But in one community where Firmus had big plans, the response was relief.

Firmus was attempting to raise cash from investors to fund its data centre plans until this week's development.

A group based in northern Tasmania, called the Environmental Awareness Association, has been campaigning against the company's three projects in the region.

Anti-data centre protesters pictured in August outside George Town Council building, ahead of the vote on whether to approve Firmus' proposed data centre. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

Nicholla Thompson from the association lives at Rowella, across the Tamar River from Firmus' proposed Bell Bay site, and said community backlash had contributed to investor concerns.

Nicholla Thompson believes community opposition to Firmus contributed to investor hesitancy. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"The dominoes are starting to fall," she said.

"They wanted it to sneak through and not be seen by people; it was thanks to the little group that we've got that really highlighted what was happening over here."

The opponents' group was relieved by the news, but was not yet celebrating it as a win for their campaign.

"A big company shouldn't be able to come in and change substantially how we choose to live in a beautiful community like this and put an AI factory up in the middle of it and have us have to endure the sound, the diesel fumes and the total destruction of our properties in value and in peace and how we live," Ms Thompson said.

Loading...

Firmus 'well-positioned' to continue plans, company says

When asked about any impact on its Tasmanian projects, a Firmus spokesperson said nothing had "fundamentally changed" about the business.

"Firmus remains well-positioned to execute on its plans, invest in its projects and serve its customers and communities, including those in Tasmania," it said.

Firmus pulls blockbuster float Firmus searches for private funding as it withdraws its application to list on the ASX just a day after closing its books to investors.

Sam Baker, from Shadforth Financial Group, said it was hard to tell if the community opposition had contributed to the IPO failing, but it would have been considered by investors.

He said it would be important to watch what Firmus did over the coming weeks and months to see if it could raise the capital.

"Firmus not being able to get this ASX listing off the ground has cast some doubt over the funding of their potential rollout of data centres in northern Tasmania," he said.

Loading Instagram content

State government optimistic

Deputy Premier Guy Barnett said the IPO was a matter for Firmus, but the Tasmanian government had been supportive "all the way through" the company's plans in the state.

"That relationship is positive and we look forward to it continuing in a collaborative, positive way," he said.

" We support investment in Tasmania, we support development, we support growth, we support more jobs. "

Data centre company's deal with AFL team defended by club boss The Tasmania Devils AFL club has signed a six-year sponsorship deal with a data centre builder.

The Tasmanian Greens said the state government should be embarrassed by its support of Firmus, saying investors, academics and communities had been raising concerns for months.

"The big question for Tasmania is why our government was so easily pulled into uncritically supporting this company despite the furiously waving red flags surrounding it," Tabatha Badger, the Greens' information and technology spokeswoman, said.

Ms Badger said the government should pause any planning decisions on Firmus's three proposals in Tasmania.

"With the ongoing questions and scrutiny that have come off the back of this failed IPO, Tasmanians have to have answers before the government proceeds any further," she said.

Firmus was also named a sponsor for Tasmania's NBL team, the JackJumpers. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

The Tasmanian-founded company had recently announced sponsorships with the Tasmania Devils AFL club, several cricket teams, including the Hobart Hurricanes, and the JackJumpers and Tasmania Jewels basketball teams.

Dr Andrew Hughes, a political marketing specialist at ANU's College of Business and Economics, said the Firmus IPO falling over was a golden opportunity for the Devils to walk away from the deal.

He said he was surprised the Devils had signed with Firmus, given the club was already exposed to community backlash over the proposed AFL stadium in Hobart.

"There was this big wedge already there, so the community is divided already and then you get a sponsor who already comes from a divided perception as well," he said.

"When they appointed Ken Hinkley as coach, they talked about community and character and care.

"I thought, 'well, hang on, if that's the things you stand for, then that's exactly what you need to look for in the sponsors and partners you grow the club with is exactly those sort of core values as well'.

"And data centres, in the minds of most people, do not say that, so it sets you back."

Premier Jeremy Rockliff has been strong in his support for Firmus' plans for Tasmania. (Supplied: Tasmanian government)

Dr Hughes said Firmus would now have a lot of work to do to rebuild trust in its brand.

"Going into a community where it's already a negative perception of that brand and then you build on it by adding some more negative to it … because your IPO, which would have funded those deals, does not go through," he said.

Dr Hughes said if the sponsorship deals with Firmus fell over, it would be harder for the clubs to re-enter the market and find new sponsors.

title: Wallabies must 'walk the walk' if 40-year-old curse is to end
text:
Arriving in Auckland ahead of the opening Bledisloe Cup Test in 1999, Wallabies great David Wilson cut a confident figure.

"We're certainly not intimidated by the All Blacks at all," said Wilson, who was acting as Wallabies captain in the absence of an injured John Eales.

Wilson was not being boastful, cocky or showing false bravado, as he had reason to declare the Wallabies were not scared of the All Blacks.

They had won all three Bledisloe Cup Tests the previous year, with the clean sweep including a famous 27-23 victory in Christchurch.

The Wallabies were also enjoying a 10-match winning streak under coach Rod Macqueen, so it was no surprise self-belief was high when they took the field on a chilly July evening at Eden Park.

What followed was later described in the Australian media as a "wake-up call" for the Wallabies.

The All Blacks stunned the Wallabies in the opening 1999 Bledisloe Cup Test at Eden Park. (Getty Images/Allsport: Nick Wilson)

They were outclassed in an error-ridden 34-15 defeat, having trailed 22-3 at half-time, with a rabid home crowd — most of whom were wearing black — doing their best to put the Wallabies off their game.

"When the Wallabies play the All Blacks in New Zealand, the contest is between a team and a nation," Spiro Zavos wrote in The Sydney Morning Herald at the time.

Given the Wallabies won the Rugby World Cup later that year, the loss was a blip on the radar.

But it did provide a salient lesson: self-belief can only take you so far when you play the All Blacks in New Zealand, as it means nothing if you cannot execute your game plan.

Wallabies upset Boks in Perth The Wallabies manage to overcome four late yellow cards to defeat world champions South Africa 42-38 in a pulsating Test in Perth.

Fast-forward to 2026, and the Wallabies find themselves faced with the same challenge as they prepare for tomorrow night's Bledisloe Cup Test, which will also be played at Eden Park.

Despite having lost their past 11 Tests against the All Blacks, expectation among the Wallabies squad is rising as they look to extend this season's six-match unbeaten run.

They posted a 42-38 victory over the Springboks in Perth a frotnight ago, while last year's stunning 38-22 defeat of the two-time defending world champions at Ellis Park is still fresh in their collective memory.

But as the 1999 Wallabies learned, confidence counts for little if you do not deliver on the field when you play the All Blacks.

"Belief is strong, but belief won't just cut it," Wallabies openside flanker Fraser McReight said earlier this week.

"We have to go out there and perform."

Eden Park 'hoodoo'

McReight would be mindful of how many times the Wallabies have made the trek to New Zealand in a buoyant mood, only to return to Australia with tail between legs.

Not since 2001 have they defeated the All Blacks in their own backyard.

Eden Park has particularly been unfriendly across Bledisloe Cup history, as the Wallabies have not triumphed over the All Blacks at the venue in 40 years.

Convincing defeats in 2008 (39-10), 2015 (41-13) and 2019 (36-0) stick out in the memory as each came a week after the Wallabies lowered the All Blacks' colours on home soil.

The Wallabies have lost 24 straight Tests to the All Blacks at Eden Park, although the New Zealanders have not been defeated by any team at their spiritual home since 1994.

Fraser McReight has stressed the Wallabies need to deliver on the field. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Suggestions of an Eden Park "curse" or "hoodoo" have resurfaced this week, as they always do whenever the Wallabies play in Auckland.

The New Zealand Herald even published an explainer on its website under the headline: A dummies' guide to the Wallabies' Eden Park hoodoo against the All Blacks — 40 years without a win.

A dictionary definition of the word hoodoo featured in the article for good measure.

Wallabies name Bledisloe Cup squad The Wallabies have kept Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing for Saturday night's Bledisloe Cup Test at Auckland's Eden Park, with Isaac Henry named in the centres.

Whether Wallabies coach Les Kiss was reading is unknown, but he maintains the run of losses has not been discussed inside his squad.

"It isn't front and centre for us in terms of what we're about," Kiss told reporters.

Instead, the Wallabies have hinted they are flipping the script.

"You can look at it two ways," McReight said.

"We're really trying to win and get the win over here … but they're also defending it [their winning record] and that has to play [on] their psyche as well.

"That's probably how we're trying to frame it."

It has been a talking point among the All Blacks, as coach Dave Rennie revealed when he announced his match-day squad on Thursday.

"No-one wants to be part of the first team for a long time to lose at Eden Park or lose the Bledisloe," said Rennie, who was sacked as Wallabies coach at the beginning of 2023.

"All sides, who come here, want to be seen to break the [Eden Park] record, so they'll [the Wallabies] be highly motivated. We're well aware of what's coming."

Dave Rennie and the All Blacks know the challenge they are facing. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

The All Blacks do not just have an envious home record at Eden Park to protect — they are also hoping to avoid four straight Test defeats.

After winning the series opener against the Springboks in Rugby's Greatest Rivalry, Rennie's side crashed to three consecutive losses.

Not since 1998 have the All Blacks dropped four Tests in a row, and the players do not need to be reminded New Zealand's rugby public only tolerates winning.

Is this the Wallabies' best chance to defeat the All Blacks on their own turf in more the two decades?

That is debatable.

The Wallabies have expressed confidence though, just as their predecessors did in 1999.

But McReight and his teammates are also aware talk is cheap.

"We don't just want to talk the talk," he said.

"We want to walk the walk and be able to deliver."

title: Woman, 71, treated on 'cold floor' of Adelaide hospital
text:
A woman has detailed how she spent four hours on the "cold floor" of an Adelaide public hospital while seeking treatment for a lung condition, calling her experience "totally wrong".

Ginny Chalmer, 71, lives with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, a condition which causes shortness of breath and impacts her oxygen levels.

The former nurse of 10 years was diagnosed earlier this year and attended a doctor on Wednesday, when her symptoms worsened after catching a virus.

She was advised her oxygen levels were low and was sent in an ambulance to Noarlunga Hospital for further treatment.

Ginny Chalmer says she does not want others to have the same experience she did at Noarlunga Hospital. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

Ms Chalmer said when she arrived, she was placed in a wheelchair and taken to a waiting room where a paramedic deemed her "fit to sit" despite telling staff she thought she was not.

She said she "felt so unwell" while sitting that she made the choice to lay down on the floor.

"At first, I was just lying on the cold floor, I didn't want to make an issue about it … then a nurse came in and asked me to get up," Ms Chalmer said.

"I said, 'no, I need to stay lying down, could you get me a blanket so I could lie on it?' and so they got me a blanket."

Ms Chalmer said she was quickly seen by a "lovely doctor" who told her she wanted to start treatment quickly — but was told the hospital did not have any beds available to put her in.

"They did bloods, they did nasal swabs and things like that [on the floor] — it wasn't that invasive, it just shouldn't happen," she said.

Ginny Chalmer was treated on the floor at Noarlunga Hospital. (ABC News: Chris Lawless)

She was also "horrified" about the privacy of other patients in the waiting room after overhearing details about people's conditions and outcomes.

"I just thought, 'wow, what about the confidentiality?'" Ms Chalmer said.

"Now, I know everything about this man that's actually sitting there, I just couldn't believe it was actually taking place."

Health network to investigate

SA Health said it had apologised to Ms Chalmer and would undertake a review of her experience.

"We do not put patients on the floor for treatment," a spokesperson said in a statement.

"On occasion, we do commence some treatment for eligible patients in the waiting room to ensure treatment can start as quickly as possible.

"The safety of our patients and staff is a key priority, and this helps reduce the time people need to wait and reduces the time people need to stay in hospital."

Jack Batty says Ginny's experience was unacceptable. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Liberal Opposition Health spokesperson Jack Batty said he was shocked to hear about Ms Chalmer's "floor care" experience and labelled it "entirely unacceptable".

"Having a 71-year-old woman lying on the ground in a public waiting room for four hours, being treated … with no privacy, is totally unacceptable," he said.

"These sorts of conditions are absolutely disgraceful — they should never take place in a system in South Australia."

Acting Health Minister Joe Szakacs said there was no mandate or practice "to treat people on our floors".

"The individual felt the need to lie down, that's entirely appropriate for her to choose to do," he said.

"Our nurses and doctors provide the care they have to provide, often in circumstances which are far from linear and far from easy.

"I think in this circumstance, the doctors and nurses involved did so in a way we should commend."

Joe Szakacs says nearly 500 people are waiting on an aged care bed in SA. (ABC News: Carl Saville)

Mr Szakacs said South Australia's hospital network remained busy for a number of reasons, including a lack of available aged care beds and rising presentations from flu cases.

"Nonetheless, the local health network is taking a look at this, I think that's also appropriate and where things can be improved or done differently ... [it] is always committed to doing that," he said.

He added that patient confidentiality was "non-negotiable" and would form part of the review.

title: Rider safety behind attempt to halt MotoGP, game developer tells court
text:
A Queensland man who is taking legal action to halt the South Australian government's plans for a MotoGP circuit has told a court he is concerned about rider safety on the proposed track.

Joshua Hogan is seeking a permanent injunction against the proposed MotoGP street circuit works, including any tree removal, in the Adelaide parklands.

Appearing in the Federal Court for the first time on Friday, a self-represented Mr Hogan said he was a game developer who loved motorsport, but it was his view rider safety concerns should be considered.

"What got me started is the safety of riders, their lives, because … they're not like a race car that has a cage or safety cells in it," he said.

"[They could possibly be] killed in a situation if the track itself is not adequate to a Grade A safety standard in the FIM (Fédération Internationale de Motocyclisme)."

The Adelaide MotoGP event is slated to start next year and would be the only street circuit in the MotoGP World Championship.

Former MotoGP world champion Wayne Gardner and motorsport journalists have previously raised concerns about rider safety on the proposed 4.13-kilometre-long circuit, which revives elements of Adelaide's old Formula One track, including the straight down Rundle Road and a corner near the Stag Hotel.

The design for the Adelaide MotoGP street circuit released in August. (Supplied: SA Government)

An SA government website states the proposed circuit design was informed by "detailed collaboration" between the SA Motor Sport Board, FIM, MotoGP and Supercars Australia, and included safety elements such as run-off areas, air fences and marshals.

"There are no compromises when it comes to rider and driver safety," the website states.

In a statement after the hearing, an SA government spokesperson said safety had been "paramount in the proposed circuit design, which has been informed by detailed collaboration".

"Experts in engineering, circuit design and motorsport safety have been engaged to guide the design," the spokesperson said.

"In addition, specialist input has been provided by former 125cc and 250cc World Champion and current MotoGP Safety Advisor Loris Capirossi and five-time Supercars champion Mark Skaife."

Mr Hogan told the court on Friday he had spent six months researching the Adelaide circuit and had found "a lot" of inconsistencies.

"I understand the timeline for a motorsport event is very tight, particularly with a circuit with this amount of importance to it, but I also feel that it's also down to rider safety," he said.

" [In] the regulations of the safety standards in the FIM, Dequetteville Terrace needed 300 metres of tarmac and it [the render] actually shows very little. It's not even close to that recommended by the safety standards of the track itself. "

An artist's impression of the Adelaide MotoGP track in the East End.

Court documents released to the ABC earlier this month showed Mr Hogan's challenge was based on similar legal arguments to those previously dismissed by the Federal Court in relation to the North Adelaide golf course upgrade.

Mr Hogan argued that the execution of plans for the MotoGP development, without being referred to the Federal Minister for the Environment, would be a breach of federal conservation laws.

Alison Doecke KC, representing the SA government, told the court on Friday that the development had been referred to the federal minister.

She said the state government anticipated "a response to the first step of that referral" between October 21 and 23, after which "early works" on the circuit would commence.

"The early site works associated with the track redevelopment will involve site establishment in late October before the Supercars event and then construction will commence immediately after the Supercar event finishes," she said.

Justice Erin Longbottom ordered Mr Hogan and the SA government to file written submissions later this month.

title: Federal government backtracks on disaster funding split
text:
The federal government has abandoned its proposed changes to disaster recovery funding, following pushback from states and councils.

In June, the government announced plans to split disaster recovery funding 50-50 with states and territories, having previously contributed up to 75 per cent in some areas.

Queensland would have felt the biggest impact — it received $1.3 billion under the current framework in 2024-25, the highest proportion in the country.

Call to drop disaster fund changes An open letter to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese claims the proposal will "bankrupt" councils, while the federal government urges their state counterparts not to "stoke fear".

Queensland's disaster recovery minister Ann Leahy this week wrote to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, calling for Canberra to abandon the proposed changes.

The letter, signed by all Queensland mayors and peak industry groups, said the changes would leave communities to fund the shortfall.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers confirmed today the federal government would keep its current cost-sharing arrangements.

Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the government wanted to provide "certainty" during disaster. (ABC News)

"This is about ensuring that the Commonwealth government is providing certainty and providing funding when disaster hits," Mr Chalmers said.

"We do take seriously all of the consultation that has happened between the government, local councils, and with other organisations to make sure that we get this right."

"Our goal here is to make sure that disaster funding can be faster, that it can be adequate and that we get the funding where it is needed as quickly as possible."

Emergency Management Minister Kristy McBain thanked councils across the country for their input on the proposal.

"I want to ensure our reforms reflect the varying experiences of communities across Australia, and these changes to the reforms will ensure no community is left behind," Ms McBain said.

"The reforms will also help ensure the system is fairer, and it's easier for councils to access funding when they need it."

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli pushed the Commonwealth to scrap the funding changes. (ABC News: Brendan Mounter)

In a statement, Queensland Premier David Crisafulli said the prime minister had listened to Queensland's concerns and made a "commonsense decision".

"We now wait to see further details, and ensure this is delivered and funding arrangements are maintained in full, so Queenslanders can have certainty and confidence in their hour of need during disaster season," the statement said.

"Today's decision diverts disaster for the most disaster-prone state.

"We look forward to strengthening our preparedness and response ahead of disaster season, in the knowledge that there will be no changes to a formula that has worked for decades."

The Local Government Association of Queensland (LGAQ) also welcomed the announcement.

"Thank you to the Commonwealth for running consultation and responding swiftly to the concerns raised by Queensland local government," LGAQ president Matt Burnett said.

"We also welcome its confirmation that councils can continue to claim costs under Counter Disaster Operations and that funding activation thresholds will be revised to ensure all communities get the support they need."

Six Queensland mayors protested a meeting about disaster funding in Melbourne in July. (ABC News)

Western Queensland Alliance of Councils [WQAC] executive officer Greg Hoffman said "it would have taken an awful long time to repair roads, bridges and other important council infrastructure" if the proposed changes had been implemented.

"The implications of the change to 50-50 from the previous 65-35 [funding split] were disastrous for the local communities if the federal government was going to walk away from that level of support,' Mr Hoffman said.

title: Dal Santo quits as St Kilda AFLW coach in winless season
text:
St Kilda's disastrous AFLW season has led to coach Nick Dal Santo stepping down after six seasons in charge, ahead of an independent review of the football program.

With four rounds to go until the end of the regular season, the Saints sit at the bottom of the AFLW ladder with eight losses from as many games.

St Kilda's percentage is a league-worst 37.2. The team is averaging 23 points per game in attack, while conceding an average of 62 points a game.

St Kilda kick solitary point St Kilda were 90 seconds from failing to score in their AFLW clash against the Western Bulldogs, as Essendon's first win of the year leaves the Saints as the only winless team in the league.

The situation reached a critical point after last weekend's game, where the Saints lost by 30 points to the Western Bulldogs in Ballarat.

Ashleigh Richards kicked a point at the 17-minute mark of the final term, for what proved the team's only score of the game.

This meant the Saints avoided becoming the first team in AFLW history not to score in a full game.

In a club announcement on Friday, St Kilda confirmed Dal Santo's decision.

Saturday's (home) match against Collingwood will be Dal Santo's final game as senior coach.

"Nick has made a significant contribution to our AFLW program across six seasons and will always be an important part of our football club," St Kilda CEO Carl Dilena said.

"His care, commitment and leadership have been unwavering, and we thank him for everything he has given to the program, including leading the team to its maiden finals appearance last season."

Winless AFLW coaches under pressure Umpiring, teams without a win and big risers: These are the topics fans are talking about midway through the AFLW 2026 season.

Dal Santo was quoted in the statement saying he was proud of "where we've been able to take this program", but that he had been giving thought to whether continuing was the right decision for him and the club.

"It's been a privilege to coach this group and help shape its formative years in the competition.

"I have a strong love for this club. I wanted to contribute to women's football, and with a daughter of my own, it's great to see a pathway for young females with football ambitions.

"I'm looking forward to finishing my time as coach alongside the group this weekend and wish them every success for what comes next."

St Kilda confirmed that football administrator and executive Brad Lloyd from Apogee Sports would lead an independent review into the program.

Lloyd has previously led reviews at AFLW clubs Richmond and Carlton.

title: The mixed fortunes of Australia's last South African touring party
text:
The members of Australia's touring party from the 2018 South Africa series have endured various fortunes in the eight years since.

Some have seen their careers go to new heights, while others struggled to recapture their form from before the ball-tampering saga.

Others never featured for Australia again.

As Australia plays its first Test in South Africa since 2018, here is a look at where everyone from the previous tour ended up in the years that followed.

Steve Smith

Steve Smith is no longer Australia's Test captain, nor is he at the peak of his powers, but he still remains the best batter in the team. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

It is somewhat of an indictment on where Australian cricket has gone since the last South Africa tour that Smith is still by far the team's best batter.

Although, a glass-half-full view might suggest that it is a sign of Smith's incredible longevity.

While he is not at the peak of his powers like he was on the last tour, Smith is still the trump card in the line-up and will be the wicket South Africa's bowlers most covet.

Smith has retired from all white ball formats and is primarily a Test cricketer at the international level.

David Warner

David Warner was not quite able to recapture his best form at the Test level following his suspension in 2018. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Arguably Australia's main antagonist in 2018, Warner last represented Australia at the T20 World Cup in mid-2024.

Following his ball-tampering suspension, Warner never quite recaptured his form, particularly in the Test format.

Warner averaged 48.63 in Tests prior to the 2018 South Africa tour and finished his career averaging 37.28 in 38 Tests afterwards.

He is now a T20 gun for hire in various competitions around the world.

Cameron Bancroft

Cameron Bancroft (left) famously fronted the press conference alongside Smith where Australia admitted to tampering with the ball using a piece of sandpaper. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

Bancroft's international career suffered the most out of the three players banned from the 2018 tour, having been the man caught by the Supersport cameras trying to hide a piece of sandpaper from the umpires.

The right-hander has played just two Tests since. The last of those came in 2019, and his Test career looks just about done.

Still just 33, Bancroft remains a prolific domestic run scorer, and ranked third in terms of runs in the Sheffield Shield last year. He has 33 first class centuries to his name.

Joe Burns

Joe Burns enjoyed a few more years of Test cricket for Australia before going on to represent Italy. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Burns was one of the players drafted into the Australian XI for the final Test in 2018 after the suspensions of Smith, Warner and Bancroft.

He enjoyed a productive 2019 at the Test level before playing the last of his Tests for Australia on Boxing Day in 2020.

Burns later became a T20 specialist for Italy, averaging 45.16 in eight matches across 2024 and 2025 to help the Italians qualify for their maiden T20 World Cup this year, but was left out of Italy's World Cup squad.

Pat Cummins

Pat Cummins has gone on to captain Australia in multiple formats since the 2018 series, where he was only just returning from a series of back issues. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Cummins's Test career was in its infancy in 2018, having just returned to the side following years of injury issues.

Since then he has become one of the finest all-format bowlers as well as Australia captain.

Under Cummins's tenure, Australia has won an ODI World Cup and the ICC Test Championship, both in 2023.

He has been named in the Test Team of the Year on four occasions, and was named Test Cricketer of the Year in 2019.

Peter Handscomb

Peter Handscomb has played fleetingly in Australia's Test side since 2018, and is seen as somewhat of a spin specialist. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Another player who came in for the final Test in 2018, Handscomb has forever been on the periphery of Australia's Test side.

Handscomb was famously the man who told the Australian team that they'd been caught ball tampering, after chatting to then-coach Darren Lehmann on a walkie-talkie while flipping an Aussie rules football in between his hands.

Considered a specialist in spinning conditions, Handscomb has added just seven Tests to his career since the 2018 series, but is an outside chance to feature again in India next year after recently being added to the Australia A side.

He was the leading scorer in the last Shield season, scoring 724 runs at an average of 34.47 in very bowler-friendly conditions.

Josh Hazlewood

Josh Hazlewood is one of the few Australians who has seen his career have an uptick following the 2018 South Africa tour. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Hazlewood enjoyed some of his best years as a Test bowler following the 2018 tour.

The right-arm paceman averaged 25.77 with the ball prior to that series and has seen that average dip to an elite 21.17 in the years that have followed.

Hazlewood is still prolific when he is able to get on the park, but his body has given him problems over the last few seasons.

The 35-year-old was restricted to just four Tests last year, but still took 16 wickets at an average of 17.93.

Jon Holland

Jon Holland played just two Tests for Australia after not featuring at all during the 2018 South Africa tour. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Holland was one of the players who didn't play a single Test during the last South Africa tour, and has mostly remained on the outer since.

His two Test appearances following the 2018 tour yielded just four wickets at an average of 75, and he was unsurprisingly surpassed in the spin pecking order.

Nevertheless, Holland continued to enjoy his time in domestic cricket, helping Victoria claim a Sheffield Shield title in 2018–19.

Holland's first class career ended in 2023 when he was let go by Victoria after 95 Shield appearances.

Usman Khawaja

Usman Khawaja completely reinvented his Test career as a prolific opener before retiring from international cricket at the start of this year. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

Khawaja played all four Tests as Australia's number three in 2018, but his struggles in that series were no indicator of what was to come.

After being left out of the Test side in 2020 and 2021, Khawaja returned for the New Year's Test in 2022 and had an incredible stint as one of Australia's openers.

Khawaja scored eight of his 16 Test centuries after his return in 2022 and averaged 48.05 as an opener, one of the best marks by an Australian.

He retired from Test cricket following Australia's Ashes triumph against England last summer and is now a T20 specialist for domestic leagues after also retiring from Shield cricket.

Nathan Lyon

Nathan Lyon still has a stranglehold on the sole spinner spot in Australia's full-strength Test XI. (Getty Images: Cricket Australia/Albert Perez)

Lyon remains a mainstay in Australia's first-choice Test XI, just as he was in 2018.

Despite being the oldest player in Australia's team, no spinner has been able to claim Lyon's spot as the non-pace bowling option alongside Starc, Hazlewood and Cummins.

Lyon's body has slowly begun to show signs of aging in the past few years, and he played just two of the five Tests against England in last summer's Ashes.

His performances in the Bangladesh Tests suggest he won't be an automatic selection in South Africa.

Mitch Marsh

Mitch Marsh retired from Test cricket after last featuring in the 2024 Boxing Day Test, but is now Australia's T20 captain. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Marsh played all four Tests against South Africa in 2018, but struggled to kick on from that series in the years that followed. He was the man with the ball in hand when the ball-tampering storm erupted.

He had a strong 2023, scoring a century and four 50s to end the calendar year with an average of 67.50, but managed an average of just 18.86 the following year and saw his Test career come to an end after Boxing Day.

Marsh has since retired from Test cricket but remains in Australia's ODI and T20 sides, captaining the country in the shortest format.

His name gets mentioned with regards to a Test return every once in a while, but that ship appears to have sailed with Australia well-stocked with all-rounder options.

Shaun Marsh

Shaun Marsh did not feature again in Australia's Test XI once Smith and Warner returned from their suspensions. (AAP Image: Dan Himbrechts)

The other Marsh brother also played all four Tests in the 2018 series, but struggled thereafter.

Marsh was relied upon heavily during the suspensions to Smith, Warner and Bancroft, but did not play another Test once the trio were cleared to return.

He played his last first class match in 2023 and his last T20 in the BBL at the end of 2024.

Marsh is one of 10 former international cricketers involved in the CLT10, India's first luxury-format indoor cricket league.

Glenn Maxwell

Despite being a key member of Australia's white ball teams, Glenn Maxwell never played another Test match after 2017. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Maxwell has not played a single Test since 2017 but remains a white ball superstar.

He played a key role in Australia's T20 World Cup and ODI World Cup wins, in 2021 and 2023 respectively.

He retired from ODIs in 2025 but still plays for Australia in the T20 format and is considered one of the most dangerous short-form players in the world.

With less international cricket on his plate, Maxwell is a gun for hire for domestic T20 leagues around the world.

Tim Paine

Tim Paine captained Australia after the ball-tampering scandal, before being forced to resign under controversial circumstances himself. (Getty: Ryan Pierse)

Paine was thrust into centre stage following the sandpaper debacle on the 2018 tour, captaining Australia in the final Test of the series in Smith and Warner's absence.

The Tasmanian keeper retained the captaincy even when Smith returned, and eventually led his country in 23 Tests.

Paine's reign as captain came to an end when he resigned in November 2021 after explicit messages he'd sent to a co-worker in 2017 resurfaced.

He ended his playing career at all levels in 2023 and took up coaching. Currently he is the head coach of Pakistan Super League side Multan Sultans.

Matt Renshaw

Matt Renshaw has only recently returned to Australia's Test side after spending years in the wilderness. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Renshaw was among those drafted into the Australian side for the final Test of the 2018 series in Johannesburg.

He played three more Tests in 2023, including one against South Africa, but managed just nine runs in four innings.

Renshaw received a Test recall earlier this year against Bangladesh, but managed just eight in his sole innings at the crease.

The left-hander has been most effective for Australia at the T20 level, where he averages 38.83 at a healthy strike rate of 125.94.

Jhye Richardson

Jhye Richardson's body has stopped him from enjoying the Test career many believed he was destined to have. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

Richardson has been the nearly man of his generation of Australian cricketers.

He did not feature in the 2018 Tests, but made his debut the following year, shining with six wickets in two Tests.

However, repeated injury issues halted his once-bright career, allowing him to play just two Tests in the last seven years.

He currently features in Australia A's Tests against India A. If his body holds up, he should be back in Test calculations in the not too distant future.

Chadd Sayers

Chadd Sayers's one Test appearance came during the final Test of the 2018 South Africa series. (Getty Images: Lee Warren)

Sayers was another one of Australia's inclusions for the Johannesburg Test in 2018, and it wound up being the only Test he would ever play.

A prolific Shield performer in the lead-up to the South Africa series, a knee injury ruined his 2018–19 season.

Sayers continued to play for South Australia and eventually retired from first class cricket at the end of the 2020–21 season.

Following his retirement, Sayers spent some time as a runner for SANFL side Woodville-West Torrens.

Mitchell Starc

Mitchell Starc remains the spearhead of Australia's bowling attack despite approaching 37 years of age. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Starc's career has gone from strength to strength since 2018, and he remains one of the most feared new ball bowlers in world cricket.

Nearly 37, Starc is as fast as ever and remains an integral part of Australia's Test line-up.

At the end of the 2018 series, Starc had taken 182 wickets at an average of 28.17 in 43 Tests.

Since then, he has taken a further 263 wickets at an average of 24.70 in 64 Tests, and his career mark of 445 Test wickets is the most by any left-arm bowler.

Share price versus offer: +6.5 per cent L1 Global Long Short Fund provided the standout transaction, launching an accelerated one-for-two non-renounceable entitlement and shortfall offer to raise up to $482.7 million. The $1.76 offer price represented a 5.9 per cent discount to the previous $1.87 close. But the real eye-catcher was the broking bench. Canaccord, E&P Capital and Taylor Collison sat at the top as joint lead arrangers and joint lead managers, backed by another seven joint lead managers – that’s right – 10 firms around one capital-raising table. Umpire! The offer was not underwritten and L1 Global wasn’t raising almost half a billion dollars to build a mine or buy an asset. It just wanted fresh ammunition for the fund’s strategy.

Advertisement

Its investment manager argued geopolitical tensions, higher bond yields and AI-driven volatility had thrown up opportunities across sectors, with plenty of stocks trading below its assessment of fair value. In other words, L1 reckoned the market’s latest bout of turbulence had thrown up a golden opportunity and wanted another $482.7 million in its war chest to take a swing at it. Or perhaps the punters just fancied beefing up their short positions as a hedge against the stratospheric gains chalked up by the hyperscaler heavyweights. The market gave the monster offer an early tick too, with L1’s offering closing at $1.875 on October 8, leaving placement punters sitting on a tidy 6.5 per cent paper profit straight out of the blocks. After the soccer team assembled for L1 Global Long Short Fund, the next heavyweight needed only two brokers. Unico Silver’s exploration and operations camp at the Joaquin silver-gold project in the Santa Cruz province of Southern Argentina.

UNICO SILVER Raised: $60 million

Price: 76c

Discount to previous close: 10.1 per cent

Current price: 67.5c

Share price versus placement: -11.2 per cent When Unico Silver went hunting for $60 million, brokers Canaccord and Euroz Hartleys duly came back with the full swag. The placement was struck at 76 cents, a 10.1 per cent discount to the previous close and 10.4 per cent below the five-day VWAP. Unico now has a pro-forma cash pile of $110 million in pro-forma cash to fund 20,000 metres of drilling across its Joaquin and Cerro Leon silver-gold projects in Argentina, with an updated resource and Joaquin’s maiden prefeasibility study set to land by January 2027.

A definitive feasibility study is pencilled in for completion by the end of 2027, with metallurgical drilling, engineering work and environmental studies set to help pave Joaquin’s path towards a final investment decision. While the brokers quietly banked $3 million for putting the $60 million away, the market was considerably less enthusiastic. By October 8, Unico was changing hands at 67.5 cents, leaving punters 11.2 per cent underwater and turning one of the biggest brokered deals of the two weeks into a double-digit aftermarket loser. And Unico wasn’t alone. MEEKA METALS

Raised: $42.4 million

Price: 10c

Current price: 8.6c

Share price versus placement: -14 per cent Meeka Metals rattled the tin at 10 cents a share and punters came charging in, snapping up 424 million shares to deliver a hefty $42.4M payday. Petra acted as sole lead manager and bookrunner for a six per cent fee on gross proceeds, pocketing an eye-catching $2.5 million. The cash was earmarked for development of the higher-grade Turnberry underground gold mine at Meeka’s Murchison gold operation, growth drilling, deferred consideration on its Mt Holland gold acquisition and working capital. The market was far less generous, marking Meeka down to 8.6 cents by October 8 and leaving the new money 14 per cent underwater.

Advertisement

Away from the headline three, AIC Mines and Kalamazoo Resources posted very different results. AIC raised $70 million at 79.5 cents through a direct strategic placement to Hawke’s Point Resource Finance to help fund its acquisition of Materra Metals’ Mt Cuthbert copper operations in Queensland. There was no conventional brokered book and no discount. By close of business on Thursday, AIC was trading at 89 cents, putting the eagle-eyed Hawke’s Point 11.9 per cent ahead on paper. Well spotted! Kalamazoo, meanwhile, pulled off a $10 million raising at 18 cents a share, a whopping 29 per cent premium to its last close. Saudi-led Muqasab SPV Holdings tipped in $7.84 million for a 9.9 per cent stake, while cornerstone investor YT International added $2.16 million. The cash will fund drilling, studies and exploration at its Ashburton gold project. Better still, Kalamazoo also stitched up the deal itself, leaving brokers empty-handed and saving a tidy sum in fees. And with the share price still sitting 20 per cent above the pre-deal close, existing shareholders have plenty to smile about too. If AIC and Kalamazoo showed you didn’t always need a broker, Mamba Exploration showed what happened when a small-cap book catches fire.

Advertisement

Mamba raised $6 million at 3.8 cents through Canaccord and Yelverton, a 15.6 per cent discount to its previous close but notably a 9.7 per cent premium to its 15-day VWAP. The pair were entitled to a six per cent fee, while Yelverton is also in line to bag 25 million corporate adviser options exercisable at six cents. The money backed a near-term 6000-metre reverse circulation program and fresh targeting across its 70 per cent-owned Meeka East copper project, where the Copper Hills and Lady Alma prospects bookend a three-kilometre corridor of historical copper mineralisation. Mamba emerged from its trading halt with a bang, trading as high as 8.2 cents, a spectacular 116 per cent above the placement price. But you had to be quick. By the October 8 close, it had retreated to 5.3 cents, still leaving thrill seekers sitting on a handsome 39.5 per cent paper gain. OD6’s Quinn fluorspar project in Nye and Lincoln counties in central Nevada, USA.

OD6 Metals brought GBA, Petra and Euroz to its $6.92 million placement party to accelerate its Quinn fluorspar project in the US, with Petra also running the book. The 9.5 cent issue price was a 13.6 per cent discount to the previous close, while the brokers shared fees of up to six per cent on broker-sourced funds and a sweet 12 million 13.3 cent options. OD6 finished at 9.6 cents, leaving the new money with its nose just 1.1 per cent above water. Felix Group provided one of the stranger pricing stories, raising $5.54 million and launching a $1 million SPP to bankroll its AI ambitions, fire up its vendor network and give its platform a further polish. Canaccord ran the book at 3.8 cents– an eye-watering 18.75 per cent premium to Felix’s previous close but a 6.5 per cent discount to its 10-day VWAP... looks like somebody had a sniff but got it wrong.

Advertisement

By October 8 the shares were back at 3.4 cents, putting placement punters 10.5 per cent underwater and turning its unusual premium-to-last-close raising into another double-digit loser. Then came some serious options firepower. DorsaVi raised $3 million at 2.2 cents to accelerate its RRAM and sensor technologies alongside a bigger push into humanoid robotics, movement data and physical-AI applications. 62 Capital picked up a six per cent fee plus a hefty 24 million broker options exercisable at 4.5 cents to grease the transaction wheels. The shares finished at 2.3 cents, leaving punters 4.5 per cent ahead. CPS raised cash for Surefire Resources even more aggressively.

Advertisement

The company’s $2.61-million placement at 1.8 cents will fund work at its Victory Bore vanadium-titanium-iron project in WA, and provide project development and working capital. CPS collected a two per cent management fee and four per cent placement fee, with a massive 31 million broker options thrown into the mix to ease the burden of getting the money into the till. For a $2.61 million raise, that was some pretty serious optionality. Surefire’s 1.9 cent close fortunately left subscribers 5.6 per cent ahead. Peregrine Gold’s $2.25 million placement at 13.5 cents was aimed squarely at putting the drill bit into the ground across its Pilbara portfolio. The program includes maiden drilling at the Coopers and Carneys iron-ore prospects, follow-up drilling and bulk sampling at its Newman gold project and first-pass drill targeting at its Mallina gold project.

Advertisement

Impressively, Mark Creasy’s Yandal Investments and Lion Selection Group cornerstoned the book, while Discovery collected a six per cent fee plus 2.5 million broker options exercisable at 20.25 cents. Peregrine finished exactly where the new money came in at 13.5 cents – no champagne, no Panadol and no gain. EcoGraf returned to the big casino with a fresh $1.175 million placement at 22.2 cents, with Canaccord in the lead-manager’s chair. The money was principally aimed at pushing the company’s Epanko graphite project in Tanzania towards financing. The new stock closed at 24 cents, leaving punters a respectable 8.1 per cent ahead. The IPO market produced just one new listing, but it gave investors plenty to smile about. Normandy Minerals hit the ASX boards on October 5 after raising $12 million at 20 cents, with Euroz as lead manager. Euroz collected a six per cent fee plus four million lead-manager options – two million exercisable at 40 cents and another two million at 60 cents.

Advertisement

The company’s projects include the Halleys gold project, which has four mineralised systems and a big 10-kilometre soil anomaly. The company also has its foot on the Halleys District gold project, which hosts multiple high-grade gold prospects and a three-kilometre-long mineralised trend. Both have seen little systematic drilling and sit roughly 130km north of Southern Cross in the WA’s Yilgarn Craton. Normandy closed at 30 cents on October 8, putting those who placed IPO bets 50 per cent ahead and giving Euroz two very different scorecards for the period: Unico investors reached for the smelling salts while Normandy punters sat pretty. At the other end of the IPO spectrum, the massive $8 billion Firmus AI data-centre float has reportedly hit the scrap heap after institutional investors baulked at its eye-watering $44 billion valuation. With established data-centre heavyweight NextDC sporting a market capitalisation of just $8 billion, Firmus appears to have pushed the valuation envelope a bridge too far. A timely reminder that even when the cheque books are wide open, investors still know when to snap them shut. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? BusinessThe economyGlobal economy Opinion An old spectre has returned to haunt Europe and things could get ugly

Mihir Sharma October 9, 2026 — 4:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. A spectre is haunting Europe: the threat of bond-market contagion. France’s fiscal failures are the source, and now even countries that were supposedly improving their finances are in danger. Italy, for one, has managed to cut its fiscal deficit, but its macroeconomic recovery is very sensitive to rising yields on its sovereign debt — and hence its borrowing costs. Years of fiscal mismanagement will cause its debt to hit 139 per cent of gross domestic product this year. The La Defense business district in Paris. A sell-off in global debt has fuelled a rout that’s hitting harder and faster in France than anyone expected. Bloomberg Trouble is brewing beyond the eurozone as well. Romania, going through another bout of political turmoil after failing to install a government on September 30, has yields of about 7.3 per cent. We’re still some distance from a repeat of the 2010-2012 eurozone crisis. But there is a reason the European Union has for a decade lurched from one emergency to another, and why every moment of stress — the 2022 loss of Russian gas, the Iran war, France’s overspending — threatens to push it over the brink. It has consistently failed in good times to prepare for the bad.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Government debt FROGS, not PIIGS, could spark the next global financial crisis Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Look beyond France at some of the bloc’s apparent successes. When you dig deeper, irresponsibility is rife. Italy is actually running a budget surplus and Giorgia Meloni’s government has stayed in power for nearly four years, giving the notoriously unstable republic an unprecedented spell of stability. But her government is still demanding that EU rules are bent to let it spend more. Countries that rack up half-decent numbers reckon that gives them licence to be irresponsible for the next few years, like dieters who think a 10-minute walk allows them to wolf down a bucket of fries. Consider the Czech Republic. Its populist billionaire leader has announced a budget that would massively increase the deficit to 3.5 per cent of gross domestic product from 2.1 per cent in 2025. Naturally, its bond yields have reached levels not seen since 2022.

Advertisement

Spain is even more disheartening. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called fresh elections, although he’s trailing badly in the polls. He has run three successive minority governments now, and perhaps hopes he can pull off an unlikely fourth win. The country is blessed by culturally compatible Spanish-speaking migrants, a climate that’s perfect for renewable energy and favourable growth numbers as a result. But there’s been no real fiscal consolidation, even though the headline deficit has fallen. Protesters in Barcelona set bins on fire during clashes with police following a demonstration over Spain’s housing crisis, hours after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced an early general election. AP The OECD points out that Spain’s structural deficit – what the deficit would be if the country grew steadily at its highest sustainable rate – isn’t declining. There’s nothing in the tank for when the engine begins to sputter. Spain typifies Europe’s problem. In times of crisis, countries look to the rest of the EU for help. In happier times they bank nothing, for themselves or the bloc.

Advertisement

Instead of being a source of strength in a struggling continent, Spain has sought to leave to others the tough job of dealing with markets, suggesting a European-level borrowing facility that could raise money on its behalf. Related Article Political unrest Tens of thousands protest housing crisis as Spain calls early election Sánchez’s attempt to introduce rent controls — which was defeated in parliament, precipitating his call for new elections — is typical. The housing shortage is a real problem, but his response was poorly thought through populism, including the automatic renewal of rental contracts. What’s needed is a genuine attempt to fix the problems that have turned Spain from a house building champion, adding 800,000 a year before the financial crisis, into a NIMBY paradise. Financial markets look at Europe and dislike what they see: a continent that hasn’t come to terms with its ageing population and the straitened finances that inevitably follow. They see patches of growth — Poland, Spain — but no sign this is being matched by the fiscal reforms that will make this growth sustainable.

Advertisement

Politicians are unable to tell electorates the truth about the necessary sacrifices, and voters refuse to believe it even when they’re told. Investors baulk at populists’ insincere and undeliverable promises, and the instability they create. Europe is an ageing continent that refuses to grow up. Above all, they see a continent-wide unwillingness to embrace the welfare and immigration reforms that might prevent stagnation. Many countries are refusing to build new homes, too, even though housing costs are crippling growth and alienating the young. No wonder bond markets are pushing yields higher. Europe is an ageing continent that refuses to grow up. It’s spending as if it’s in the first flush of youth, without the earning capacity to justify that.

title: A novella about dementia finds poetry in the spaces where words fail
text:

CultureBooksLiterature A novella about dementia finds poetry in the spaces where words fail Susan Wyndham October 9, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Carrie Tiffany was anxious when she flew from Melbourne to visit the artist Noel McKenna at his Sydney studio. “I’m always nervous about meeting people for the first time and he’s someone I hold in high regard,” she says. “The first thing we did was talk to the dogs, and then we went out to the balcony to look at the butcherbird. So we were slightly communicating through the animals.” This was the ideal introduction for two animal-loving, creative introverts. “We’re definitely not out there,” says the laconic McKenna. They were collaborating on Tiffany’s new book, The Lady with the Dog, which tells the story of an old woman with dementia whose confusion and loss of language are filtered through an old dog. Words and images travelled in quiet dialogue between Tiffany’s house by the Yarra river and McKenna’s home-studio at Rose Bay. Author Carrie Tiffany and artist Noel McKenna have collaborated on The Lady and the Dog. Sam Mooy She has always written about odd but ordinary characters and their animals in exquisite short novels: Everyman’s Rules for Scientific Living (2005), Mateship with Birds (2012) and Exploded View (2019). At just 10,000 words, the new one is described by her publisher as a novella and by Tiffany as “possibly an imaginative biography”, based on her own mother’s experience. “I’m a miniaturist in all things and the big world annoys me,” she says. “I’ve always looked at things close up. For me it’s very difficult to do something in a story that is wholly original. We’re all working on the seven plots. But it’s exciting what you can do in a sentence that is completely in and of itself, and you can put it next to another sentence and create these strange juxtapositions and reverberations.”

Advertisement

Photo: McKenna’s ink drawings perfectly fill out the 100-page hardback book and the spaces in the woman’s mind that words can’t express. “We’re both sort of distilling complicated things to make the essence,” he says. McKenna, too, is a celebrated artist of everyday domestic life with a timeless nostalgia and gentle humour. He paints lone figures in sparse rooms shared with cats, dogs, birds and horses. He listens to music – Talking Heads or Michael Jackson – and his old dogs, Melman the greyhound and Rosie the Jack Russell terrier, are always nearby. The National Portrait Gallery paired McKenna with the 20th-century artist John Brack for a recent exhibition highlighting their wry social commentary. Another recent show in Sydney was titled Memory. Tiffany has a strong visual sense and has written essays about contemporary artists. Like McKenna, she admires the assemblages of American artist Joseph Cornell and they both make collages. She first saw McKenna’s art – in an image of a racehorse – on the cover of Gerald Murnane’s essay collection Invisible Yet Enduring Lilacs. Her partner, the New Zealander writer Lloyd Jones, gave her a painting by McKenna called Fish Talking to Horse. McKenna was the artist she wanted to work with on her book. “I read the story at different times and I could see images coming,” McKenna says. “There were connections with me, with my brother having Alzheimer’s, with the dog, and there’s a black stove mentioned quite a bit. I immediately thought of this outsider artist in America called James Castle who was a deaf mute and spent his whole life making drawings, mainly with soot and spit. I love his work, and that got my interest.”

Advertisement

By chance, there have been seven-year gaps between all Tiffany’s books, which have won many awards, including the first Stella Prize, and twice she was shortlisted for the Miles Franklin. She has always written slowly, while raising her daughter and son, and working with farmers and environmentalists as editor of Landcare magazine. Now she is a full-time lecturer in English and creative writing at La Trobe University. She has a new grandchild and travels between Melbourne and Auckland with Jones, whose home is on Waiheke Island. They married there two years ago after being separated by the pandemic. (Reading Madame Bovary together on Zoom helped to connect them.) One of Noel McKenna’s illustrations for Carrie Tiffany’s deeply personal book. Sam Mooy COVID also brought worse complications. Tiffany grew up in Perth with her mother, brother and stepfather, and left at 16 to work as a park ranger in the Northern Territory. She felt a terrible mixture of guilt and relief at not being able to visit during Western Australia’s two-year border closure. Her mother had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and, wanting a small dog for company, ended up with Sally, “a smelly old German shepherd”. Her stepfather had built a “Colditz-style fence” around the property to prevent them from wandering. The phone was the only link between mother and daughter. “I would always start our phone conversations with ‘How is the dog?’ It seemed to be the main way that we could say something to each other. In the last few weeks we would have some sweet, strange conversations, and often when the noun was missing I would insert ‘dog’. So we had a lot of strange conversations about dogs.”

Advertisement

By the time Tiffany caught the first possible plane to Perth, her stepfather had suffered a near-fatal heart attack and been taken to hospital, and her mother had been admitted to a psychiatric hospital. All she could do was be with them as they died; first her stepfather and, weeks later, her mother. He had done his stoical best to look after her in their grim isolation. “We’re both sort of distilling complicated things to make the essence,” McKenna says of his collaboration with Tiffany. Sam Mooy She found the dog another home and cleared the house, which was cluttered with meaningless piles her mother had placed in every room: bank statements, pegs, jelly beans, dentures, cake forks, coins, Christmas decorations. Angry with the West Australian government for sacrificing vulnerable old people to a hardline policy, she thought about writing something for a newspaper. “But perhaps I’m not that sort of writer,” she says. “I always need distance to make sense of things. About a year later I realised I wanted to write about her confusion and about the dog.” While cleaning the house she had re-read Anton Chekhov’s short story The Lady with the Dog, about a banker who falls in love with a young woman he sees with her little dog, and their adulterous affair. Tiffany sees her novella as an oblique homage to Chekhov’s sad love story. “I realised that I was thinking of that fateful woman as my mother, and I felt that her life had been fateful,” she says. “Things happened to her when she was a young woman that really set things in stone for her and made her life much more constrained and difficult as she got older. This played into her dementia in ways I felt awful about because I think a lot of the time she was trapped in autobiographical memory.”

Advertisement

Related Article Literature Barbara Kingsolver’s hymn to Appalachia and the healing power of art Tiffany’s story was even shorter until she added some of her mother’s memories of being sent to live with her grandmother after her father returned from war, her early unhappy marriage, and the dogs scattered throughout her life. Also, she says, “for a writer, the thing that happens in language is fascinating – the gap where the word doesn’t exist can be quite poetic because it can let all this other meaning flow into that gap”. The woman in the story scrambles her words, speaking of her “pressing gown” and “snifferchiefs”. The pages have dashes, empty spaces and McKenna’s drawings. They show the woman and dog circled by a fence, and the woman with a question mark; the dog watching a spider, or a huge, pointing finger. Most disconcerting are an upside-down clock and two clocks with different times. Doctors ask people with dementia to draw a clock face, and their jumbled numbers can be “heartbreaking but also beautiful”, Tiffany says. “They seem to be denying time, which is the thing you don’t have when you have Alzheimer’s.” Much of the work on Tiffany’s short books is beneath the finely honed surface. But there may not be a seven-year wait for the next one. She has almost finished a novel partly inspired by the Canberra artist Rosalie Gascoigne’s timber triptych Suddenly the Lake. “It’s about an older couple and I think it’s an erotic novel,” she says with amused shock. “We’ll see.”
