Let’s get this straight. Australia should want big, bold technology companies, and it should want them listed here where ordinary investors can share in the upside. But Firmus was always going to be a hard sell. Just after 9am on Friday, it stopped trying. The data centre start-up withdrew its $43.7 billion sharemarket float, which would have been the largest on the ASX since Telstra in 1997, after big investors refused to pay its price. Firmus co-founders Tim Rosenfield and Oliver Curtis. Matt Willis Firmus builds what it calls AI factories: data centres packed with Nvidia chips, whose computing power it rents to tech giants such as Meta and OpenAI to run their AI. Unlike most data centre operators, which rent out space and power, it owns the chips itself. Most of those factories do not exist yet. Firmus runs two data centres, in Melbourne and Singapore, with seven more contracted and four in planning. Of the 912 megawatts of computing capacity it has signed customers up for, just 46 are running: about 5 per cent.

Advertisement

The company asked Australians to buy a skyscraper off the plan. For once, the market asked to see the foundations first. Is this the AI bubble bursting? Not on this evidence. Spending on AI is still climbing, and chip giant Nvidia announced a $US150 billion share buyback late last month. But investors are getting pickier. Smart-ring maker Oura has delayed its US float, and shares in CoreWeave, Firmus’ closest listed rival, have halved in a year. The ramifications are significant for its two chief architects – cousins who were set to be instant billionaires and had no real experience in the technology sector – and will sweep across Australia’s AI sector and the economy more broadly. Had Firmus listed this month, millions of Australians would most likely have ended up owning a slice of it through their super, without ever being asked. They won’t now. The float was supposed to complete one of the more remarkable comebacks in Australian business for Oliver Curtis, Firmus’ 40-year-old co-chief executive.

Advertisement

The comeback that wasn’t Oliver Curtis and Roxy Jacenko. The float was supposed to complete one of the more remarkable comebacks in Australian business. Oliver Curtis, Firmus’ 40-year-old co-chief executive and the husband of public relations entrepreneur Roxy Jacenko, is a former investment banker who served a year in jail for insider trading a decade ago. He has since called his actions “incredibly, gravely stupid”. He co-founded Firmus in 2019 as a bitcoin mining business with his cousin Tim Rosenfield, who ran a luxury lingerie brand, and Jonathan Levee, who handles the engineering. Neither co-chief executive came from the technology industry. They signed up big names all the same. Nvidia, the world’s most valuable chipmaker, is a shareholder and James Packer and former treasurer Joe Hockey hold stakes. “As a father, I’m incredibly proud of what Oli’s done,” Curtis’ father Nick, a mining entrepreneur and major shareholder, told The Australian last week.

Advertisement

Firmus earned about $US50 million ($73 million) in revenue last financial year. It asked to be valued at about 600 times that. “Investors just weren’t prepared to pay a sky-high price up-front for capacity that’s still largely on the drawing board,” Josh Gilbert, who analyses Asia-Pacific markets for investing platform eToro, told this masthead. Related Article Updated

AI Oliver Curtis’ bid to float Firmus for $44 billion falls over The price had climbed quickly. Firmus sought a $1.2 billion valuation in late 2024 and raised money at $15 billion in August. Then it asked public investors for almost three times that. The road to Friday was rocky, to put it lightly. This week Firmus confirmed that a $73 billion partnership with CDC, an established Australian data centre operator, was over. The Financial Review reported that a test of Firmus’ prized cooling system had flooded part of CDC’s Melbourne data centre earlier this year.

Advertisement

David Allen, who runs a fund at investment manager Plato that bets on shares falling, said the price assumed Firmus would “execute almost flawlessly” and grow its revenue by about 25,300 per cent in three years. Fund managers who met the founders before the float told the Financial Review that their interest could drift quickly when an investor wasn’t a believer. David Allen, who runs a fund at investment manager Plato that bets on shares falling, said the price assumed Firmus would “execute almost flawlessly” and grow its revenue by about 25,300 per cent in three years. Eamon Gallagher The country’s biggest super funds, including Aware Super, UniSuper and Australian Retirement Trust, stayed out. “Firmus is such an unknown quantity,” said Ben Squires, who invests the retirement savings of teachers and community workers at NGS Super. Even then, investors already holding Firmus, including Nvidia and US investment giants Blackstone and Coatue, could have sold about $17 billion of existing shares from the first day of trading. That is more than twice the $7.9 billion new investors were being asked to put in.

Advertisement

‘Bankers gone to ground’ Related Article Analysis

IPO Oliver Curtis’ transformation from jailbird to corporate kingpin has gone awry The banks running the float, JPMorgan, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and Morgans, told investors on Monday that demand at $11 a share was “well in excess” of what was on offer. One Morgans adviser emailed clients that demand had been “enormous”. By Wednesday, the banks were discussing cutting the price to about $9. On Thursday morning, they told fund managers that bids made that morning were “not held”, then went quiet. “Bankers gone to ground,” read one message doing the rounds of brokers and investors. By midday the offer documents had been pulled from view. ASIC has dealt with this kind of message before, extracting a court-enforceable undertaking from Goldman Sachs in 2018 over how it described demand for a share sale. The regulator declined to comment on Firmus.

Advertisement

Who pays now Whether Firmus can recover from here is an open question. The Australian reported on Friday that Firmus is drawing up plans to list on America’s Nasdaq exchange next year. Until then, it will need private money, and the deepest pockets around it belong to Nvidia, Blackstone and Coatue. Their deal this year entitles them to extra shares if Firmus has not listed by November 30. Every one of those shrinks the founders’ slice. The Australian reported on Friday that Firmus is drawing up plans to list on America’s Nasdaq exchange next year. Bloomberg Curtis owns about 13 per cent of the company. title: They booked a cheap cruise package. Then the tickets vanished
text:
When Brisbane resident Harry Harding found a sold-out cruise deal online, he was sceptical.

The eight-night Carnival Cruise sailing from Brisbane to Vanuatu and other Pacific destinations had already sold out in the cabin category he and his housemate wanted.

Then they came across an advertisement on RedNote, a Chinese social media platform, claiming cabins were still available.

Harding spent time checking the seller before handing over any money.

"There were lots of comments on the RedNote account saying the service was good and reliable, so we trusted them," he told SBS Chinese.

After paying a 10 per cent deposit, the pair received what appeared to be legitimate tickets. Confident the booking was genuine, Harding's housemate transferred the remaining balance — about US$2,500, or more than AUD$3,500.

The booking appeared on Carnival's website. Their names were attached to it. They could log in, buy Wi-Fi packages and reserve restaurants.

"It just seemed legitimate," he said.

Then, less than a week before they were due to leave, everything disappeared.

READ MORE Think you can spot scam red flags? The warning signs are changing

"About six days before we were due to leave, we noticed the booking was gone," he said.

"From that point, they largely stopped responding to us and would just say things like, 'Please be patient'."

When Harding contacted Carnival, he says he was unable to get answers because the booking had been made using someone else's payment details.

"Because the travel agent had booked the tickets with a different credit card, the person on the hotline wouldn't give me any information for privacy reasons," he said.

Harry did his due diligence on this travel agent. But he was still scammed on a pricey Carnival Cruise holiday. Source: Supplied / SBS Chinese

"So even though it was our names and our passport numbers on the tickets, we couldn't actually do anything through Carnival."

The situation became even more complicated because the travel agent was based overseas.

"The travel agency was a Chinese travel agent and they booked the tickets through the American office of Carnival," he said.

"We're in Australia, so basically had no recourse because nobody here in Australia could help us."

Lured in by big discounts

Brisbane resident Lucy Liu says she had a similar experience.

She and three other passengers booked a five-day cruise after finding what appeared to be a heavily discounted fare through a Chinese travel agent.

The cabin was advertised for about $1,300, compared with around $1,800 on the cruise line's website.

"It was around a 30 per cent discount," Liu told SBS Chinese.

"They told us it was a last-minute promotional price, and that was what attracted us."

Like Harding, Liu believed the business appeared legitimate.

Lucy thought she was buying tickets on a cruise from a reputable seller. She later discovered Beijing authorities had revoked the company's business licence. Source: Supplied / SBS Chinese

The RedNote account carried platform verification and displayed a business licence and company name.

"They had also displayed their business licence and company name on the account," she said.

But shortly before departure, Liu learned the booking had been cancelled.

When she sought an explanation, she received conflicting answers.

"At first they blamed us, saying we had entered our information incorrectly and that the cruise company couldn't contact us, which was why the booking was cancelled," she said.

"Then someone else said it was cancelled because we hadn't checked in."

According to Liu, the cruise line advised that the payment had been reversed and the money returned to the original account used to make the booking.

Liu says she later discovered information online showing the travel company's licence had reportedly been revoked by authorities in Beijing.

Both Lucy and Harry were targeted by what appeared to be a "sophisticated" travel scam after they tried to purchase cheaper tickets for a Carnival Cruise. Source: Getty / South Florida Sun-Sentinel/TNS

"The biggest difficulty, in my view, is probably related to cross-border consumer protection," she said.

"We weren't really sure which authority we should approach to resolve the issue."

How does this happen?

Melbourne-based cruise travel agent Snow Yu, who has worked in the industry for 14 years, says heavily discounted cruise fares can be a warning sign.

"They use very low advertised prices as a hook," she told SBS Chinese.

Yu says scammers have previously focused on highly sought-after Disney cruises before shifting their attention to brands including Royal Caribbean and Carnival.

She believes cases like these may involve fraudulent payment methods.

"It could be the result of credit card fraud," she said.

"After the cardholder discovers the transaction, they may report the card or transaction to the bank and recover the money."

"Once that payment is recovered, the cruise company has to cancel the booking.

"The problem isn't necessarily the booking itself, but the method of payment."

Carnival Cruise Line told SBS Chinese that travel scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated.

"Unfortunately, travel scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated, and we urge guests to exercise caution when purchasing a holiday through third parties," a spokesperson said.

"Guests should only book directly through Carnival Cruise Line or through reputable, accredited travel agents."

Melbourne commercial lawyer Tina Ji says consumers should be cautious if they're asked to transfer money directly or make advance payments outside established booking systems.

"Potential warning signs include requests for advance payment or requests to make private/direct transfers," she said.

Ji said people involved in disputes through platforms such as WeChat or RedNote should first consider reporting the matter through those platforms, noting that cross-border cases can raise jurisdictional challenges.

Yu recommends checking industry bodies such as the Australian Travel Industry Association and Cruise Lines International Association to help verify whether a travel agent is legitimate.

'Believe the official website'

Harding and his housemate eventually recovered their money after publicly challenging the travel agent online.

He says affected customers began comparing notes and found what appeared to be links between multiple accounts advertising cruise deals under different names.

"We knew that whoever was doing this was repeating the scam just under a different name," he said.

The business would repeat the scam under different names, Harry and other consumers found. Source: Supplied / SBS Chinese

Harding posted comments warning other consumers and uploaded a video naming the travel agency.

"But in the end, because of all the pressure that we were placing on them, they did eventually refund us on the condition that we would remove the posts," he said.

"As of this day, I have not removed my post."

His advice to other travellers is simple.

"If somebody is offering you a ticket to something and it says it's sold out on the official website, believe the official website," he said.

"Don't believe the person who's trying to sell you something."

SBS Chinese contacted the travel agency involved for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.

title: The 65-year-old Greek club taking on A-League giants in sold-out Australia Cup final
text:
IN BRIEF: The South Melbourne Hellas will face Melbourne Victory this weekend in a colossal Australia Cup final.

Each team has their own storied history and represent 'old' and 'new' football in Australia.

It's a sold-out football final 12 years in the making, but with roots that go back decades, as South Melbourne take on Melbourne Victory.

The first all-Victorian Australia Cup final of the modern era will bring together two giants of Australian football representing different generations.

At Melbourne's Rectangular Stadium, four-time A-League champions Melbourne Victory will face the South Melbourne Hellas — four-time National Soccer League champions and the third non-A-League team to make an Australia Cup final.

South Melbourne, a 65-year-old club founded by Greeks, boasts former Socceroos coach Ange Postecoglou and one of football's best ever players Ferenc Puskás as alumni.

The team got here largely thanks to 25-year-old striker Bul Juach, who proved the hero in last month's semi-final, coming off the bench to score a second-half hat-trick in the 3-1 win over Queensland Lions.

Bul, nicknamed the 'Raging Bul' told SBS News, "It's a good feeling. It's massive for the club. You can see the morale, and everyone is happy."

"The boys have been welcoming. The club has been welcoming ... I just have to keep going well, and hopefully we can win some trophies."

At 12, the South Sudanese Australian migrated to Canberra, where he began playing organised sport.

"Before that it was street football," he said.

Juach said that football helped him through the adjustment of migrating to Australia, including learning the language and the culture.

"It was a big change coming from Africa, but football helped me a lot," he said.

"It's the world game — it's for everyone. That is the beauty of it."

The winner will claim silverware and a berth in next year's Asian Champions League 2, whilst South Melbourne are hoping a win will boost their cause as they seek inclusion to the A-League.

A multicultural legacy

Juach said it was "good to see" multiculturalism in the South Melbourne club.

"That is what all of Australia is about," he said.

"We are all proud to be representing this club. We can see how big it is and the ambition of the club, and we all want to be part of that."

Founded by Greek immigrants in 1959, the South Melbourne club amalgamated three clubs: South Melbourne United, Hellenic and Yarra Park.

Behind the merger was Theo Marmaras, along with Georgios Samaras, the grandfather of the former Celtic and Greece striker of the same name.

Despite the club's rich Greek diaspora connection, history and influence, Juach is today part of a diverse playing group — reflecting the sport's multiculturalism at a national level.

Ask about Socceroos of African heritage, Juach said players such as Awer Mabil, Thomas Deng, Nestory Irankunda and Mohamed Toure were an inspiration to the African community.

"Big pride. It’s all good to push the younger generation to aim for bigger things and play at these levels and stages," he said.

Two football giants of different generations

Originally called the FFA Cup, the fixture was launched in 2014 and is now known as the Australia Cup.

This season's campaign involved 777 clubs from across Australia.

Melbourne Victory has previously lifted the trophy in this competition in 2015 and 2021, both at Melbourne Rectangular Stadium, and finished runners-up to Macarthur FC at the same venue in 2024.

The A-League giants go into this final without marquee Spanish player Juan Mata, who has left the club, and under new Venezuelan coach Giovanni Savarese, appointed in June this year.

In a statement, Football Australia chief executive officer Martin Kugeler said, "Both clubs have proud histories and passionate supporter bases."

The governing body's executive director of football, Heather Garriock, said the tournament has "meant a lot to the NPL and community clubs across the country".

South Melbourne represents the traditional NPL system and a club history stretching decades, while Melbourne Victory represents the professional A-League, which started in 2005, a year after the NSL folded.

A-League entities such as Melbourne Victory, Adelaide United and Sydney FC built their own modern history. Meanwhile, legacy clubs such as South Melbourne, Heidelberg, Sydney Olympic and Marconi were relegated to state leagues, demanding a return to the national spotlight ever since.

South Melbourne captain Marco Jankovic said he was looking forward to the "special day".

title: How the ATO found itself embroiled in a battle over credit cards that forced a rethink
text:
Key Points A ban on credit card payments for tax bills has been pushed back to June 2027.

This change is one of three shifts made in October to how money moves.

The federal government has been forced to delay the Australian Taxation Office's (ATO) planned ban on the use of credit cards to pay tax bills until June 2027, following a backlash from business groups.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers announced additional funding for the ATO on Friday to maintain the payment option until at least June 2027, after critics argued the ban puts pressure on small businesses that rely on credit cards to manage cash flow.

The decision to delay was an unintended consequence of the government's broader payments reforms, which included a ban on card surcharges and lower transaction fees.

Here's how the controversy unfolded.

What has changed?

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The ATO's move is linked to a broader shake-up of Australia's payments system that took effect this month.

First card surcharges were banned. Second, the rate banks charge businesses to transfer money from customers to businesses was cut from 0.8 per cent to 0.3 per cent. Thirdly, EFTPOS, Mastercard and Visa must publish the merchant fees they charge so businesses can compare rates and avoid paying higher-than-average fees.

The fourth change flows from the lower fees banks charge on transactions because they subsidise frequent flyer and rewards points programs. Banks started raising annual fees and offering fewer perks ahead of the rate changes.

Why did the ATO make the change?

The decision followed the Reserve Bank's ban on surcharges for EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard payments, which began on 1 October. The ATO said continuing to accept credit cards and absorbing the processing fees would cost about $200 million annually.

The ATO "explored options" including with credit card companies to seek lower fees, but they did not offer fees low enough to allow the ATO to afford to continue to accept credit card payments.

Other government departments, including Border Force and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, say they will continue to accept credit card payments.

The ATO has said it will continue to consult with "relevant stakeholders and stewardship groups to understand how best to support those experiencing financial hardship and identify alternative arrangements for businesses and individuals who are unable to pay via other methods."

Why were people angry?

Some small businesses use credit cards to bridge or extend the gap between when a tax bill is due and having to pay it. Losing this option means finding cash sooner or arranging alternative finance. Credit cards can offer rewards such as frequent flyer points when they are used.

Business groups said there was a double standard because they have to accept cards and absorb the fees or raise prices, while the tax office simply withdrew the option to pay by card entirely. They also say the consultation period was too rushed, with just two months to adapt and raise concerns.

Why is it political?

Labor promoted the surcharge ban as a cost of living relief, but the ATO's response caused a small business backlash and the government's response was contradictory.

Ministers Anne Aly and Clare O’Neil urged further engagement and said a workable solution must be found for small businesses because they had "real concerns" about the ATO's move before the extended deadline.

Meanwhile, the Coalition pushed for the ban to be reversed. Opposition leader Angus Taylor said the government should force the ATO to reverse the decision on Friday, before the treasurer did so.

READ MORE Card surcharges are banned. Now Aussies are fuming over another charge

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson, speaking on Friday before the backflip, said, the ATO "needs to overturn its ban because this is a situation of complete inconsistency between the standard set for small business and the standard set for the Australian Taxation Office imposed by the Albanese government".

How many people are affected?

The latest ATO data shows about 2.3 per cent of tax payments were made with credit cards in the 2024/25 financial year, most of them coming from privately owned wealthy groups, and public and multinational businesses.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief Andrew McKellar said the sector was worried and angry.

"There's 4.9 million small businesses out there — active small businesses. Even if this only affects ... around 5 per cent of all of those businesses, that's a quarter of a million individual small businesses who are directly inconvenienced by this," he said.

What happens now?

Treasurer Jim Chalmers announced extra funding for the ATO to delay the credit card ban until June 2027.

After 30 June 2027, the ATO will continue to accept credit card payments via third parties as well as other free and low-fee payment methods like debit card and bank transfer.

"We will continue to work closely with small businesses and the ATO on this issue to get the best outcome," Chalmers said.

title: The Block has run into an unexpected problem ahead of its new season
text:
in brief Dozens of cats are believed to be living on and around The Block's next build site in Melbourne's north-west.

Advocates are seeking a pathway to trap, treat and rehome them.

Heritage concerns aren't the only challenge facing The Block's next build, with a population of unowned cats becoming the latest flash point.

Animal welfare advocates have urged the television network behind the reality television series to step up and help rescue the feral felines — dozens of which are believed to be living on and around the site in Sunbury in Melbourne's north-west.

The Nine Network says it is aware of the cats living at Jackson's Hill, which formerly housed an asylum and psychiatric hospital, and is assessing the situation.

The cats are currently cared for by a group of volunteers, who hope to reach an agreement with the local council, Hume City Council, to legally rescue and rehome them.

SBS News has contacted Hume City Council for comment.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Under Victoria's Domestic Animals Act, the management of feral cats — which have a significant impact on wildlife — is typically the responsibility of local councils, unless they are on crown land, like in national parks, where the duty is shared with the state government.

When cats are collected by council pounds or rescue shelters, they muust be held for eight days before they can be rehomed, or if necessary, euthanised.

The holding period for euthanasia doesn't apply to cats that are deemed "wild, uncontrollable or diseased".

The Nine Network says it is aware of the cats. Source: Supplied

State Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell has written to Nine and The Block, calling for a comprehensive welfare plan to coordinate rescue and veterinary support for the cats.

"While The Block isn't responsible for causing this problem, they can be part of the solution, and this is a chance for them to show some goodwill to the community, respect for animals rather than just profiting off development," she said.

"Site clearing, demolition, construction traffic, fencing and the broader transformation of the site will only disturb and displace these cats and make any rescue attempts even harder."

Three buildings at Sunbury's former psychiatric hospital will be redeveloped in The Block's 2027 season. Source: Supplied / Victorian Heritage Council

Purcell said at minimum, the show should fund veterinary assessments and provide financial assistance to foster carers for the cats.

Under Victoria's framework, independent rescuers are often left to manage financial, logistical and legal risk, where shelters are unable to take entire colonies.

A spokesperson for Nine said the network was aware of the cats near the site and was "assessing the situation prior to their safe removal" and the start of construction, slated for the new year.

"We intend to keep all relevant stakeholders engaged throughout this process," the spokesperson said.

Volunteer rescuers want a clear legal pathway to manage established cat colonies to enable humane trapping, veterinary treatment including desexing and rehoming, without people having to bear the risks.

READ MORE What Australia's feral cat crisis reveals about the fight to save native wildlife

The Cat Protection Society of Victoria, which is not aware of this particular colony but rehomes around 600 to 700 stray cats a year, said doing this sort of work requires significant help from volunteers.

"Most strays also require behavioural work, some quite substantial. We're very fortunate to be supported by a cat-loving community who provide volunteer hours and financial assistance," the society's operations manager Alison Thompson said.

The upcoming Block season has already faced backlash from the local community over concerns about the site's historical significance.

In 1864, the site, then known as Caloola, opened as an industrial school, according to the Victorian Heritage Register. Over the next century, it was redeveloped as an asylum, then a psychiatric hospital, and later as a training centre for people with disabilities.

Victoria University was given some of the site in 1944, but stopped using it as a campus in 2009. The Victorian goverment bought the site in 2018 to "return most of it to community use", according to the state's transport and planning department.

An application for adaptive re-use and conservation to create six private residences, adding swimming pools and undercover parking has been lodged with Heritage Victoria. The regulator has extended submissions for community engagement.

title: Why the Russian plague lab case is unlikely to cause the next pandemic
text:
IN BRIEF The cause of Darya Shipilova's fatal pneumonia remains unknown as Russia denies risk of further outbreak.

Experts say an plague outbreak in Australia is 'extremely unlikely', but more information is crucial.

Limited facts and circulating misinformation have fuelled international panic about the death of a Russian lab worker from an unidentified source of pneumonia. But Australian experts say there's no threat of a global health crisis.

Darya Shipilova, an employee at the Russian Anti-Plague Research Institute in Irkutsk, southern Siberia, died in early October after contracting pneumonia, Russian health authorities have said.

Despite introducing sweeping preventative health measures, they have since said that there is no further risk to the population.

However, limited information has been released about the cause of the 28-year-old's pneumonia, and the World Health Organization (WHO) is seeking further answers from Russia.

The Australian Centre for Disease Control (CDC) told SBS News there is "no evidence to suggest an increased risk to the Australian public from this event at this time".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The organisation said that while it's aware of the death, "verified information remains limited".

"The Australian CDC is engaged through established international public health networks and is monitoring the situation closely," it said. "We will continue to assess the situation as further information becomes available."

Associate Professor Suman Majumdar, chief health officer at Melbourne's Burnet Institute, a leading scientific research centre, told SBS News there is "no reason for Australians to be alarmed".

"At this stage, we have a serious and unusual death with unanswered questions, but we do not have evidence of a plague outbreak, or a risk to Australia," he said.

Russia's health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, confirmed Shipilova's death on 2 October, two days after she became ill.

READ MORE The telltale sign Russia's plague scare could be more serious

It confirmed she was vaccinated and was "immune to the dangerous infections with which she worked".

Pneumonia is a lung infection that can be caused by a variety of conditions, including plague, flu, or COVID-19. There has been no information released clarifying what caused Shipilova's pneumonia or how she contracted the illness.

Rospotrebnadzor said there is no danger of an outbreak, with almost 200 people quarantined in preventative measures.

"As of October 7, 2026, medical monitoring has been completed for over 90 per cent of contacts," the agency said.

"No health issues related to infectious diseases were detected, and the result of nearly 5,000 laboratory tests revealed no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms."

Infectious disease expert and clinical microbiologist, Professor Paul Griffin said it's "concerning" that Shipilova worked in a laboratory with the Yersinia pestis bacteria, which causes the plague. The same bacteria was responsible for the Black Death that killed tens of millions of people in Europe between 1346 and 1353.

"There's no confirmation that is related to her work, but we also haven't heard or seen the actual results of the testing to verify that — or the results to say what she actually passed away from," he said.

"We certainly do need more information, but at this stage it doesn't seem like this is something that's not going to be able to be readily contained."

'Transparent information sharing' crucial to global safety

This lack of information has concerned the WHO, which initially deemed the death to be a low risk to global public health.

However, it has since changed its messaging.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment," said WHO director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

"Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential risks".

WHO department of epidemic and pandemic management director, Maria Van Kerkhove said the organisation wants "more information to understand which laboratory tests were conducted, which pathogens were evaluated".

She said if Russia confirmed Shipilova did not die from the plague, the cause of the fatal pneumonia should be determined and that information shared.

Kerkhove said the WHO had contacted Russia's health ministry requesting "further answers".

Russia denies it has not fully informed the WHO about the death, saying it has provided information "in accordance with established practice".

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov claimed the media was responsible for circulating misinformation and causing concern.

Griffin said the lack of information sharing may result from "perception issues and other potential sensitivities geopolitically".

"It's difficult to know what the motives would be for not providing the information required."

The microbiologist said "transparent, real-time, open disclosure" is needed to "allay everyone's concerns".

'No evidence' of another pandemic

Majumdar from the Burnet Institute said that the "lack of information" about the cause of Shipilova's pneumonia is "not evidence that a larger outbreak is occurring".

While Shipilova worked in an anti-plague laboratory, both Griffin and Majumdar said there's no chance that an outbreak of the plague would be as serious or severe as the COVID-19 pandemic.

"There are literally no parallels that are reasonable to COVID-19," Griffin said.

He said that typically seven people die in the United States annually from the plague.

"It's not something that's gone away ... this organism has been around for many hundreds, if not thousands of years. We know a lot about it. It's nowhere near as easily transmissible as COVID."

READ MORE What we know about the mysterious death at a Russian plague institute

Majumdar said the bacterial infection can be easily treated.

"We have diagnostic tests and treatments. Antibiotics are effective, particularly when treatment begins early, and people who have been exposed can also be given antibiotics before they develop symptoms," he said.

"Unlike COVID-19 or influenza, the plague is not known for widespread sustained community transmission from people with mild or no symptoms."

According to Griffin, Australia's health system and laboratory safety standards are "so robust" that an outbreak or incident is "so extremely unlikely".

"If it were to happen, our systems would kick in so swiftly to ensure the safety of everyone involved, including potential contacts," he said.

"We would be on the front foot by communicating this to relevant authorities and the public to make sure there was no undue alarm."

title: 'Exposed for the sham it is': Celebrations as High Court blocks major coal mine expansion
text:
IN BRIEF: The High Court has ruled against a major coal mine expansion in NSW.

Campaigners have welcomed the first case to consider broad environmental impacts.

Australia's highest court has upheld a first-of-its-kind environmental challenge to overturn a major coal mine expansion, after a years-long community campaign in east-central NSW.

In a landmark decision on Wednesday, the High Court ruled against the proposed expansion of the Mount Pleasant coal mine near Muswellbrook, in the Upper Hunter region of NSW.

It is the first time a court has upheld that project approvals must account for the broad environmental impacts of burning fossil fuels.

Environmental campaigners have termed the decision a victory for all Australians and called on the government to move away from fossil fuels.

Australian resource company MACH Energy sought to extend the life of Mount Pleasant coal mine in NSW by 22 years — to 2048 — and nearly double its yearly output to 22 million tonnes of carbon dioxide per year.

The state planning commission approved the proposal in 2022 before local Hunter Valley residents launched a legal challenge.

While the first bid to block the expansion was dismissed, in 2025, the NSW Court of Appeal unanimously ruled the approval unlawful, after it found planning authorities are legally required to consider the climate impact of Scope 3 emissions on local communities.

Scope 3 emissions are classified as indirect emissions tied to a company's broader business activities by the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, the top international standard for measuring greenhouse gas emissions.

MACH Energy took the finding to the High Court, which struck down the appeal on Wednesday morning.

The company said while it was "disappointed" with the outcome, it accepts the court's decision and "will carefully review the judgment to understand its implications for future project assessments and environmental approvals."

Mining approvals for the coal mine were due to end in November, before an August approval offered a lifeline from the state government, allowing for a continuation of operations to the end of 2032, as well as an increase in the approved extraction rate from 10.5 to 12.5 million tonnes of coal per year.

A years-long fight

The original case was brought by Wendy Wales, a retired science teacher and the president of the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG).

On Wednesday, she said the ruling acknowledged the risks to Australians posed by climate-influencing activities.

"This ruling acknowledges that many Australian communities have already suffered extreme weather devastation," she said.

"Now the true and complete long-term costs of export coal on Australians, via the climate impact from burning that coal, must be considered."

DAMSHEG said the proposed coal mine extension would generate 870 million tonnes of carbon dioxide, 98 per cent of it from coal burned overseas.

Greens spokesperson for climate change and planning Sue Higginson said the court had "exposed the New South Wales coal approval process for the sham it is, and declared that new coal cannot be approved when 98 per cent of the climate pollution are ignored".

"The High Court have sided with the climate science and declared that the NSW Independent Planning Commission was wrong to ignore downstream emissions when approving a massive new coal project."

A legal precedent in NSW

The High Court upheld the refusal of the planning commission's Mount Pleasant plan approval because the scope 3 emissions were not properly assessed.

"By majority, the High Court held the (planning) commission had failed to consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, specifically 'scope three' emissions as required (by law)," the court said in a summary.

Head of climate and energy at Greenpeace Australia Pacific, Joe Rafalowicz, called on the Australian government, as well as leaders at COP31, to find the "courage, leadership and grit" to move away from fossil fuels, adding that the ruling clearly set a binding precedent for environmental challenges in the state.

"It is legally imperative that all of the pollution from fossil fuel projects be considered before approving a new project."

Rafalowicz said it was a victory for Australians "bearing the brunt" of extreme weather fuelled by fossil fuel corporations.

"Coal and gas companies have claimed they are not responsible for their pollution because it happens overseas, but today Australia’s highest court sided with common sense and scientific evidence to find that every new coal and gas approval in this country could put us at risk, no matter where it is sold or burnt."

READ MORE The two-metre question that could wipe out a population

The Minerals Council of Australia said the decision was a "further blow" to Australia's prospects of meeting continued demand from global customers for our "high-quality coal".

"Developing a coal mine in Australia is already difficult enough because of long approval times, lawfare by activists and high royalties and other taxes," Minerals Council of Australia chief executive officer Tania Constable said in a statement.

"The decision sends a very negative signal to Australia’s trade and investment partners about sovereign risk in this market."

The council said resource companies should not be "forced into a situation where well-funded legal attacks over a number of years require a High Court appeal", adding that legal challenges "seek to game the legal system by creating uncertainty and delay without ever having to pay costs".

"Investors in Australia’s resource sector will carefully review the outcome from today’s High Court judgement."

title: 'I want to be here the rest of my life': Lionel Messi's emotional international retirement
text:
In brief Footballer Lionel Messi has played his final international match, scoring in a 3-0 win over Benin.

Messi announced he would retire from international matches following Argentina's World Cup final loss to Spain.

Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his 21-year international career on Wednesday, bidding farewell to adoring Argentina fans in an emotional final appearance for the former world champions in Buenos Aires.

In a perfectly scripted finale, the 39-year-old widely regarded as the greatest football player in history signed off with his 126th international goal in front of 85,000 supporters as Argentina cruised to a 3-0 victory over Benin.

Messi, playing in his record-extending 208th international, also provided the assist for the opening goal scored by veteran Nicolas Otamendi, with Nico Paz also scoring.

But the match was a footnote to the occasion itself, which saw Messi savouring the adulation of the Monumental Stadium crowd one last time for an event which had been billed as 'The Last Tango'.

"It was a huge source of pride for me to defend this jersey for more than 20 years," Messi told fans in a post-match address.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Not coming anymore is going to be deeply painful. I swear I'd like to play for the rest of my life, because playing for the Argentina national team is the most beautiful thing that can happen to you."

Messi, though, said he had no regrets about his decision to retire, citing Argentina's gruelling World Cup campaign, which took place as his late father was seriously ill, as a factor.

"Even though I want to be here all my life, I feel that this is the moment. The last World Cup was too much, everything I had to live through," said Messi.

Beforehand, Messi wiped away tears as the bus carrying him and his Argentina teammates made its way through crowds of well-wishers en route to the stadium.

Messi took the field alongside his three children and received affectionate waves from his wife, Antonela Roccuzzo, and his mother, Celia Cuccittini, who were watching from a VIP box.

Shortly before kick-off, a giant Argentina jersey bearing the word "Gracias" (Thank You) above the football superstar's No.10 was laid out on the pitch as the crowd roared their approval.

Messi welled up again as Falklands War veteran Fabio Santana sang the national anthem beside a banner which read "The Malvinas are Argentine", the same banner held aloft by players after their 2-1 World Cup semi-final win over England.

The match was halted in the 10th minute — a tribute to Messi's famous shirt number — for a minute-long ovation to the former Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain star.

He crowned the occasion with a goal from the penalty spot in the 71st minute.

'Gave it my all'

At the final whistle, a drone show lit up the night sky above the stadium, showing Messi's image and thanking the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner for his career.

Messi's farewell came two and a half months after Argentina's World Cup final defeat to Spain in New Jersey, where Messi exited in tears after making little impression in an ill-tempered 1-0 loss.

"I gave it my all; I have nothing left to give, and besides, there are great young players coming up who deserve their chance," Messi wrote at the time.

Before Wednesday's game, the University of Buenos Aires awarded Messi an honorary doctorate in a ceremony at the Argentine Football Association (AFA) headquarters.

Messi, who has in the past spoken of his regret at not studying more, expressed pride at the distinction.

"To be able to say that I am an honorary doctor!" he joked.

Outside the Argentina Football Association headquarters, fans unfurled a huge Argentine flag with his image inscribed "The joy of my life."

Former Barcelona teammate and Brazil's all-time top goalscorer Neymar paid tribute to the departing champion on X.

"It's not just Argentina that thanks you, the world thanks you for everything you did for football. Thank you for making me love football even more," he said.

Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami in the US's Major League Soccer league until 2028, although following the death of his father, Jorge, two months ago, he revealed he may hang up his boots for good sooner than anticipated.

Messi's departure comes four years after his greatest triumph in international football, leading Argentina to victory at the 2022 World Cup to end the country's 36-year wait for a third title, cementing his status as Diego Maradona's heir.

"I believe Messi gave everything, absolutely everything, so it doesn't bother me at all that he's leaving. He has more than earned it, let him enjoy himself, let him rest," Cecilia Adriano, 52, told a reporter from the Agence France-Presse news agency.

During his time with the Albiceleste, Argentina won one World Cup, were runners-up twice (Brazil 2014 and North America 2026) and were also crowned Copa America champions in 2021 and 2024.

Big Hits looks at notable drill hits reported to the ASX this week, with Dalaroo Metals stealing the show and Power Minerals and Midas Minerals snapping at its heels. So let’s dive in. DALAROO METALS LTD (ASX: DAL) Project: Bondoukou gold ridge project, Côte d’Ivoire Hit: 18m at 7.31g/t gold from 63m downhole.

Grassroots exploration triumphs are the lifeblood of junior resource players, and this week Dalaroo Metals claimed the top step on the podium after turning a compelling structural story targeting a distinct magnetic geophysical corridor into a premier West African gold discovery. Undertaking the first-ever drilling campaign across its highly prospective terrain in north-eastern Côte d’Ivoire, the company delivered spectacular high-grade bedrock intercepts from the very first fence of holes put into its Wilfred target. The headline reverse circulation hole punched through strongly silicified volcaniclastic rock to return 18 metres at 7.31 grams per tonne gold (g/t) from a depth of 63 metres downhole. Highlighting the robust grade distribution within the core of this system, every single one-metre sample within the interval returned more than 1.72g/t gold, with a peak individual assay roaring up to 15.9g/t gold from a depth of 78m. What makes the performance globally significant is that the gold mineralisation appears broad, continuous, and remarkably shallow. A second ‘scissor’ hole, drilled from the opposite direction to confirm the target’s structural architecture, successfully collared near-surface oxide mineralisation, returning 23 metres at 2.14g/t gold from surface. Together, the first two scissored holes successfully intersected gold from both directions across multiple fresh rock and oxide zones. This spectacular double-strike provides immediate confirmation of a well-developed, structurally controlled gold system sitting within the prominent Birimian greenstone belt, a prolific geological province in Côte d’Ivoire endowed with many multi-million-ounce gold deposits.

Advertisement

The commercial appeal of the project is underscored by the immense scale of the target corridor, which has seen its footprint grow rapidly to an estimated seven kilometres of strike length, following the company’s soil sampling and shallow auger drilling campaigns. The newly defined corridor incorporates the company’s priority Mag, Wilfred, and Ali targets, which sit right at the heart of an active exploration district just 35 kilometres from other major regional operations. With a massive exploration runway, these breakthrough results represent only the opening salvo of a bigger 102-hole broadside against the task ahead. Dalaroo’s drill rods are spinning around the clock on day and night shifts, with a hefty backlog of assays still to come as the company charges towards a potential maiden mineral resource estimate. Dalaroo Metals’ maiden reverse circulation drill program has delivered high-grade bedrock gold along a fresh seven-kilometre corridor at its Bondoukou project. POWER MINERALS LTD (ASX: PNN)

Advertisement

Project: Morro do Ferro rare earths project, Brazil Hit: 119m at 4.94 per cent total rare earth oxides from surface Securing second place on the Big Hits podium is Power Minerals, which has dramatically amplified the commercial scale of its South American critical minerals strategy with a truly massive rare earths intersection. Stepping out with a major resource definition campaign at its flagship project in Brazil, the company demonstrated the immense tonnage potential of the Morro do Ferro prospect by logging an exceptionally thick, high-grade mineralised envelope. The standout diamond hole delivered a continuous, bulk-tonnage run of 119 metres at 4.94 per cent total rare earth oxides (TREO), beginning directly from surface.

Advertisement

The intercept represents an outstanding accumulation of shallow mineralisation, backed up by a second deep hole on the same section that returned 98 metres at 5.09 per cent TREO, further reinforcing the exceptional grade consistency of this deposit. Crucially for the economics of the project, the massive geological system is heavily enriched with the highly valuable chemical elements required to fuel the global energy transition. The initial 119-metre surface interval carried a premium magnet rare earth oxide (MREO) grade of 0.89 per cent, or 8906 parts per million (ppm), which represents a vital volume of the essential elements neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium. Within the broader mineralised body, tighter high-grade zones continue to emerge at depth, highlighted by a rich 10-metre interval at 12.31 per cent TREO from 41 metres downhole, packing a hefty 1.88 per cent – or 18,789ppm MREO. The consistent thickness and exceptional grade profile recorded from the surface position the deposit as an incredibly cost-effective, bulk-tonnage target with negligible overburden.

The company is rapidly progressing its engineering and trade-off studies to capitalise on the deposit’s shallow regolith architecture. Concurrently, the company is undertaking metallurgical testwork alongside the expanded diamond program, providing a strong technical foundation as the project moves rapidly toward a landmark resource update over the coming months. MIDAS MINERALS LTD. (ASX: MM1) Project: Otavi copper-silver project, Namibia Hit: 22.6m at 4.67 per cent copper and 70.9g/t silver from 347.5m Midas Minerals rounds out the podium with third place for this week, successfully broadening the commercial parameters of its African base metals portfolio by uncovering high-grade extensions at its premium Otavi project in Namibia.

Targeting the outer margins of the known high-grade part of the deposit’s Main Zone, step-out diamond drilling shattered previous structural limits by intercepting broad, high-grade base metal and silver mineralisation. The breakthrough hole delivered a strong downhole composite of 22.6 metres assaying 6.01 per cent copper equivalent, which comprised a length-weighted average of 4.67 per cent copper and 70.9 grams per tonne (g/t) silver from a depth of 347.5 metres. The broad intercept is anchored by an exceptionally rich interior core which returned an outstanding 10 metres going 11.55 per cent copper equivalent from 355.5 metres depth downhole. The discovery of those high-grade extensions on the edges of the central deposit is structurally significant for the junior explorer. It provides definitive evidence that the hydrothermal copper-silver system remains open, well-developed and expanding laterally well beyond the boundaries of the previous geological model. A second step-out hole on a separate traverse successfully mirrored this lateral continuity, returning a wide intercept of 33.2 metres at 2.51 per cent copper equivalent from 310.3 metres, further confirming that major mineralised zones extend into previously undrilled blocks.

The company has established a commanding exploration position across the highly endowed Otavi copper belt, a premier mining jurisdiction in Namibia featuring excellent regional infrastructure and ready proximity to operating processing facilities. By proving that the richest parts of the copper-rich system continue to step out laterally, the current campaign has materially de-risked Midas’ geological model. The company has seven operational drill rigs on site, with an eighth rig slated to join the fleet shortly. This drilling capacity will be invaluable to Midas’ aggressive extensional and regional targeting across a robust prospect pipeline through the end of the final quarter. This edition of Cap Raise Crucible follows more than $700 million of ASX raising action, with brokers banking fees and options, while punters count the winners and losers. The capital-raising conveyor belt kept rolling over the past fortnight, though one monster transaction did most of the heavy lifting. More than $700 million was chased down across the raising universe, with L1 Global Long Short Fund’s $482.7 million entitlement offer accounting for the lion’s share. And if the money was concentrated, the broking action wasn’t. Canaccord Genuity, E&P Capital and Taylor Collison landed the plum roles as joint lead arrangers and joint lead managers to the L1 Global offer, while Ord Minnett, Morgans, Shaw and Partners, CommSec, Bell Potter, MST Financial Services and NAB piled in as joint lead managers.

Advertisement

Further down the food chain, Euroz Hartleys, Petra Capital, GBA Capital, Yelverton Capital, Blue Ocean Equities, 62 Capital, CPS Capital, Discovery Capital, Prenzler and Peak Asset Management all found their way onto tickets. Some brokers picked up healthy cash fees. Others scored millions of options. Meanwhile, AIC Mines and Kalamazoo Resources showed the broking fraternity wasn’t necessary, pulling in $70 million and $10 million respectively without a broker in sight. As a corporate hound, getting your name on the tombstone is only half the test. The other is what happened afterwards and whether punters ended up drinking champagne or reaching for the Panadol. By the October 8 close, results ranged from double-digit losses to spectacular wins, including one placement that briefly more than doubled the new money. L1 GLOBAL LONG SHORT FUND

Advertisement

Raised: Up to $482.7 million

Structure: Accelerated one-for-two non-renounceable entitlement offer plus shortfall

Price: $1.76

Discount to previous close: 5.9 per cent

Current price: $1.875

Share price versus offer: +6.5 per cent L1 Global Long Short Fund provided the standout transaction, launching an accelerated one-for-two non-renounceable entitlement and shortfall offer to raise up to $482.7 million. The $1.76 offer price represented a 5.9 per cent discount to the previous $1.87 close. But the real eye-catcher was the broking bench. Canaccord, E&P Capital and Taylor Collison sat at the top as joint lead arrangers and joint lead managers, backed by another seven joint lead managers – that’s right – 10 firms around one capital-raising table. Umpire! The offer was not underwritten and L1 Global wasn’t raising almost half a billion dollars to build a mine or buy an asset. It just wanted fresh ammunition for the fund’s strategy.

Advertisement

Its investment manager argued geopolitical tensions, higher bond yields and AI-driven volatility had thrown up opportunities across sectors, with plenty of stocks trading below its assessment of fair value. In other words, L1 reckoned the market’s latest bout of turbulence had thrown up a golden opportunity and wanted another $482.7 million in its war chest to take a swing at it. Or perhaps the punters just fancied beefing up their short positions as a hedge against the stratospheric gains chalked up by the hyperscaler heavyweights. The market gave the monster offer an early tick too, with L1’s offering closing at $1.875 on October 8, leaving placement punters sitting on a tidy 6.5 per cent paper profit straight out of the blocks. After the soccer team assembled for L1 Global Long Short Fund, the next heavyweight needed only two brokers. Unico Silver’s exploration and operations camp at the Joaquin silver-gold project in the Santa Cruz province of Southern Argentina.

Advertisement

UNICO SILVER Raised: $60 million

Price: 76c

Discount to previous close: 10.1 per cent

Current price: 67.5c

Share price versus placement: -11.2 per cent When Unico Silver went hunting for $60 million, brokers Canaccord and Euroz Hartleys duly came back with the full swag. The placement was struck at 76 cents, a 10.1 per cent discount to the previous close and 10.4 per cent below the five-day VWAP. Unico now has a pro-forma cash pile of $110 million in pro-forma cash to fund 20,000 metres of drilling across its Joaquin and Cerro Leon silver-gold projects in Argentina, with an updated resource and Joaquin’s maiden prefeasibility study set to land by January 2027.

Advertisement

A definitive feasibility study is pencilled in for completion by the end of 2027, with metallurgical drilling, engineering work and environmental studies set to help pave Joaquin’s path towards a final investment decision. While the brokers quietly banked $3 million for putting the $60 million away, the market was considerably less enthusiastic. By October 8, Unico was changing hands at 67.5 cents, leaving punters 11.2 per cent underwater and turning one of the biggest brokered deals of the two weeks into a double-digit aftermarket loser. And Unico wasn’t alone. MEEKA METALS

Advertisement

Raised: $42.4 million

Price: 10c

Current price: 8.6c

Share price versus placement: -14 per cent Meeka Metals rattled the tin at 10 cents a share and punters came charging in, snapping up 424 million shares to deliver a hefty $42.4M payday. Petra acted as sole lead manager and bookrunner for a six per cent fee on gross proceeds, pocketing an eye-catching $2.5 million. The cash was earmarked for development of the higher-grade Turnberry underground gold mine at Meeka’s Murchison gold operation, growth drilling, deferred consideration on its Mt Holland gold acquisition and working capital. The market was far less generous, marking Meeka down to 8.6 cents by October 8 and leaving the new money 14 per cent underwater.

Advertisement

Away from the headline three, AIC Mines and Kalamazoo Resources posted very different results. AIC raised $70 million at 79.5 cents through a direct strategic placement to Hawke’s Point Resource Finance to help fund its acquisition of Materra Metals’ Mt Cuthbert copper operations in Queensland. There was no conventional brokered book and no discount. By close of business on Thursday, AIC was trading at 89 cents, putting the eagle-eyed Hawke’s Point 11.9 per cent ahead on paper. Well spotted! Kalamazoo, meanwhile, pulled off a $10 million raising at 18 cents a share, a whopping 29 per cent premium to its last close. Saudi-led Muqasab SPV Holdings tipped in $7.84 million for a 9.9 per cent stake, while cornerstone investor YT International added $2.16 million. The cash will fund drilling, studies and exploration at its Ashburton gold project. Better still, Kalamazoo also stitched up the deal itself, leaving brokers empty-handed and saving a tidy sum in fees. And with the share price still sitting 20 per cent above the pre-deal close, existing shareholders have plenty to smile about too. If AIC and Kalamazoo showed you didn’t always need a broker, Mamba Exploration showed what happened when a small-cap book catches fire.

Advertisement

Mamba raised $6 million at 3.8 cents through Canaccord and Yelverton, a 15.6 per cent discount to its previous close but notably a 9.7 per cent premium to its 15-day VWAP. The pair were entitled to a six per cent fee, while Yelverton is also in line to bag 25 million corporate adviser options exercisable at six cents. The money backed a near-term 6000-metre reverse circulation program and fresh targeting across its 70 per cent-owned Meeka East copper project, where the Copper Hills and Lady Alma prospects bookend a three-kilometre corridor of historical copper mineralisation. Mamba emerged from its trading halt with a bang, trading as high as 8.2 cents, a spectacular 116 per cent above the placement price. But you had to be quick. By the October 8 close, it had retreated to 5.3 cents, still leaving thrill seekers sitting on a handsome 39.5 per cent paper gain. OD6’s Quinn fluorspar project in Nye and Lincoln counties in central Nevada, USA.

Advertisement

OD6 Metals brought GBA, Petra and Euroz to its $6.92 million placement party to accelerate its Quinn fluorspar project in the US, with Petra also running the book. The 9.5 cent issue price was a 13.6 per cent discount to the previous close, while the brokers shared fees of up to six per cent on broker-sourced funds and a sweet 12 million 13.3 cent options. OD6 finished at 9.6 cents, leaving the new money with its nose just 1.1 per cent above water. Felix Group provided one of the stranger pricing stories, raising $5.54 million and launching a $1 million SPP to bankroll its AI ambitions, fire up its vendor network and give its platform a further polish. Canaccord ran the book at 3.8 cents– an eye-watering 18.75 per cent premium to Felix’s previous close but a 6.5 per cent discount to its 10-day VWAP... looks like somebody had a sniff but got it wrong.

Advertisement

By October 8 the shares were back at 3.4 cents, putting placement punters 10.5 per cent underwater and turning its unusual premium-to-last-close raising into another double-digit loser. Then came some serious options firepower. DorsaVi raised $3 million at 2.2 cents to accelerate its RRAM and sensor technologies alongside a bigger push into humanoid robotics, movement data and physical-AI applications. 62 Capital picked up a six per cent fee plus a hefty 24 million broker options exercisable at 4.5 cents to grease the transaction wheels. The shares finished at 2.3 cents, leaving punters 4.5 per cent ahead. CPS raised cash for Surefire Resources even more aggressively.

The company’s $2.61-million placement at 1.8 cents will fund work at its Victory Bore vanadium-titanium-iron project in WA, and provide project development and working capital. A spectre is haunting Europe: the threat of bond-market contagion. France’s fiscal failures are the source, and now even countries that were supposedly improving their finances are in danger. Italy, for one, has managed to cut its fiscal deficit, but its macroeconomic recovery is very sensitive to rising yields on its sovereign debt — and hence its borrowing costs. Years of fiscal mismanagement will cause its debt to hit 139 per cent of gross domestic product this year. The La Defense business district in Paris. A sell-off in global debt has fuelled a rout that’s hitting harder and faster in France than anyone expected. Bloomberg Trouble is brewing beyond the eurozone as well. Romania, going through another bout of political turmoil after failing to install a government on September 30, has yields of about 7.3 per cent. We’re still some distance from a repeat of the 2010-2012 eurozone crisis. But there is a reason the European Union has for a decade lurched from one emergency to another, and why every moment of stress — the 2022 loss of Russian gas, the Iran war, France’s overspending — threatens to push it over the brink. It has consistently failed in good times to prepare for the bad.

Advertisement

Related Article Opinion

Government debt FROGS, not PIIGS, could spark the next global financial crisis Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Look beyond France at some of the bloc’s apparent successes. When you dig deeper, irresponsibility is rife. Italy is actually running a budget surplus and Giorgia Meloni’s government has stayed in power for nearly four years, giving the notoriously unstable republic an unprecedented spell of stability. But her government is still demanding that EU rules are bent to let it spend more. Countries that rack up half-decent numbers reckon that gives them licence to be irresponsible for the next few years, like dieters who think a 10-minute walk allows them to wolf down a bucket of fries. Consider the Czech Republic. Its populist billionaire leader has announced a budget that would massively increase the deficit to 3.5 per cent of gross domestic product from 2.1 per cent in 2025. Naturally, its bond yields have reached levels not seen since 2022.

Advertisement

Spain is even more disheartening. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called fresh elections, although he’s trailing badly in the polls. He has run three successive minority governments now, and perhaps hopes he can pull off an unlikely fourth win. The country is blessed by culturally compatible Spanish-speaking migrants, a climate that’s perfect for renewable energy and favourable growth numbers as a result. But there’s been no real fiscal consolidation, even though the headline deficit has fallen. Protesters in Barcelona set bins on fire during clashes with police following a demonstration over Spain’s housing crisis, hours after Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez announced an early general election. AP The OECD points out that Spain’s structural deficit – what the deficit would be if the country grew steadily at its highest sustainable rate – isn’t declining. There’s nothing in the tank for when the engine begins to sputter. Spain typifies Europe’s problem. In times of crisis, countries look to the rest of the EU for help. In happier times they bank nothing, for themselves or the bloc.

Advertisement

Instead of being a source of strength in a struggling continent, Spain has sought to leave to others the tough job of dealing with markets, suggesting a European-level borrowing facility that could raise money on its behalf. Related Article Political unrest Tens of thousands protest housing crisis as Spain calls early election Sánchez’s attempt to introduce rent controls — which was defeated in parliament, precipitating his call for new elections — is typical. The housing shortage is a real problem, but his response was poorly thought through populism, including the automatic renewal of rental contracts. What’s needed is a genuine attempt to fix the problems that have turned Spain from a house building champion, adding 800,000 a year before the financial crisis, into a NIMBY paradise. Financial markets look at Europe and dislike what they see: a continent that hasn’t come to terms with its ageing population and the straitened finances that inevitably follow. They see patches of growth — Poland, Spain — but no sign this is being matched by the fiscal reforms that will make this growth sustainable.

Advertisement

Politicians are unable to tell electorates the truth about the necessary sacrifices, and voters refuse to believe it even when they’re told. Investors baulk at populists’ insincere and undeliverable promises, and the instability they create. Europe is an ageing continent that refuses to grow up. Above all, they see a continent-wide unwillingness to embrace the welfare and immigration reforms that might prevent stagnation. Many countries are refusing to build new homes, too, even though housing costs are crippling growth and alienating the young. No wonder bond markets are pushing yields higher. Europe is an ageing continent that refuses to grow up. It’s spending as if it’s in the first flush of youth, without the earning capacity to justify that.

title: A novella about dementia finds poetry in the spaces where words fail
text:

CultureBooksLiterature A novella about dementia finds poetry in the spaces where words fail Susan Wyndham October 9, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Carrie Tiffany was anxious when she flew from Melbourne to visit the artist Noel McKenna at his Sydney studio. “I’m always nervous about meeting people for the first time and he’s someone I hold in high regard,” she says. “The first thing we did was talk to the dogs, and then we went out to the balcony to look at the butcherbird. So we were slightly communicating through the animals.” This was the ideal introduction for two animal-loving, creative introverts. “We’re definitely not out there,” says the laconic McKenna. They were collaborating on Tiffany’s new book, The Lady with the Dog, which tells the story of an old woman with dementia whose confusion and loss of language are filtered through an old dog. Words and images travelled in quiet dialogue between Tiffany’s house by the Yarra river and McKenna’s home-studio at Rose Bay. Author Carrie Tiffany and artist Noel McKenna have collaborated on The Lady and the Dog. Sam Mooy She has always written about odd but ordinary characters and their animals in exquisite short novels: Everyman’s Rules for Scientific Living (2005), Mateship with Birds (2012) and Exploded View (2019). At just 10,000 words, the new one is described by her publisher as a novella and by Tiffany as “possibly an imaginative biography”, based on her own mother’s experience. “I’m a miniaturist in all things and the big world annoys me,” she says. “I’ve always looked at things close up. For me it’s very difficult to do something in a story that is wholly original. We’re all working on the seven plots. But it’s exciting what you can do in a sentence that is completely in and of itself, and you can put it next to another sentence and create these strange juxtapositions and reverberations.”

Advertisement

Photo: McKenna’s ink drawings perfectly fill out the 100-page hardback book and the spaces in the woman’s mind that words can’t express. “We’re both sort of distilling complicated things to make the essence,” he says. McKenna, too, is a celebrated artist of everyday domestic life with a timeless nostalgia and gentle humour. He paints lone figures in sparse rooms shared with cats, dogs, birds and horses. He listens to music – Talking Heads or Michael Jackson – and his old dogs, Melman the greyhound and Rosie the Jack Russell terrier, are always nearby. The National Portrait Gallery paired McKenna with the 20th-century artist John Brack for a recent exhibition highlighting their wry social commentary. Another recent show in Sydney was titled Memory. Tiffany has a strong visual sense and has written essays about contemporary artists. Like McKenna, she admires the assemblages of American artist Joseph Cornell and they both make collages. She first saw McKenna’s art – in an image of a racehorse – on the cover of Gerald Murnane’s essay collection Invisible Yet Enduring Lilacs. Her partner, the New Zealander writer Lloyd Jones, gave her a painting by McKenna called Fish Talking to Horse. McKenna was the artist she wanted to work with on her book. “I read the story at different times and I could see images coming,” McKenna says. “There were connections with me, with my brother having Alzheimer’s, with the dog, and there’s a black stove mentioned quite a bit. I immediately thought of this outsider artist in America called James Castle who was a deaf mute and spent his whole life making drawings, mainly with soot and spit. I love his work, and that got my interest.”

Advertisement

By chance, there have been seven-year gaps between all Tiffany’s books, which have won many awards, including the first Stella Prize, and twice she was shortlisted for the Miles Franklin. She has always written slowly, while raising her daughter and son, and working with farmers and environmentalists as editor of Landcare magazine. Now she is a full-time lecturer in English and creative writing at La Trobe University. She has a new grandchild and travels between Melbourne and Auckland with Jones, whose home is on Waiheke Island. They married there two years ago after being separated by the pandemic. (Reading Madame Bovary together on Zoom helped to connect them.) One of Noel McKenna’s illustrations for Carrie Tiffany’s deeply personal book. Sam Mooy COVID also brought worse complications. Tiffany grew up in Perth with her mother, brother and stepfather, and left at 16 to work as a park ranger in the Northern Territory. She felt a terrible mixture of guilt and relief at not being able to visit during Western Australia’s two-year border closure. Her mother had been diagnosed with Alzheimer’s and, wanting a small dog for company, ended up with Sally, “a smelly old German shepherd”. Her stepfather had built a “Colditz-style fence” around the property to prevent them from wandering. The phone was the only link between mother and daughter. “I would always start our phone conversations with ‘How is the dog?’ It seemed to be the main way that we could say something to each other. In the last few weeks we would have some sweet, strange conversations, and often when the noun was missing I would insert ‘dog’. So we had a lot of strange conversations about dogs.”

Advertisement

By the time Tiffany caught the first possible plane to Perth, her stepfather had suffered a near-fatal heart attack and been taken to hospital, and her mother had been admitted to a psychiatric hospital. All she could do was be with them as they died; first her stepfather and, weeks later, her mother. He had done his stoical best to look after her in their grim isolation. “We’re both sort of distilling complicated things to make the essence,” McKenna says of his collaboration with Tiffany. Sam Mooy She found the dog another home and cleared the house, which was cluttered with meaningless piles her mother had placed in every room: bank statements, pegs, jelly beans, dentures, cake forks, coins, Christmas decorations. Angry with the West Australian government for sacrificing vulnerable old people to a hardline policy, she thought about writing something for a newspaper. “But perhaps I’m not that sort of writer,” she says. “I always need distance to make sense of things. About a year later I realised I wanted to write about her confusion and about the dog.” While cleaning the house she had re-read Anton Chekhov’s short story The Lady with the Dog, about a banker who falls in love with a young woman he sees with her little dog, and their adulterous affair. Tiffany sees her novella as an oblique homage to Chekhov’s sad love story. “I realised that I was thinking of that fateful woman as my mother, and I felt that her life had been fateful,” she says. “Things happened to her when she was a young woman that really set things in stone for her and made her life much more constrained and difficult as she got older. This played into her dementia in ways I felt awful about because I think a lot of the time she was trapped in autobiographical memory.”

Advertisement

Related Article Literature Barbara Kingsolver’s hymn to Appalachia and the healing power of art Tiffany’s story was even shorter until she added some of her mother’s memories of being sent to live with her grandmother after her father returned from war, her early unhappy marriage, and the dogs scattered throughout her life. Also, she says, “for a writer, the thing that happens in language is fascinating – the gap where the word doesn’t exist can be quite poetic because it can let all this other meaning flow into that gap”. The woman in the story scrambles her words, speaking of her “pressing gown” and “snifferchiefs”. The pages have dashes, empty spaces and McKenna’s drawings. They show the woman and dog circled by a fence, and the woman with a question mark; the dog watching a spider, or a huge, pointing finger. Most disconcerting are an upside-down clock and two clocks with different times. Doctors ask people with dementia to draw a clock face, and their jumbled numbers can be “heartbreaking but also beautiful”, Tiffany says. “They seem to be denying time, which is the thing you don’t have when you have Alzheimer’s.” Much of the work on Tiffany’s short books is beneath the finely honed surface. But there may not be a seven-year wait for the next one. She has almost finished a novel partly inspired by the Canberra artist Rosalie Gascoigne’s timber triptych Suddenly the Lake. “It’s about an older couple and I think it’s an erotic novel,” she says with amused shock. “We’ll see.”
